landmarks.name: Attara Kacheri
landmarks.description: Attara Kacheri is the red-ochre neoclassical building opposite the Vidhana Soudha on Ambedkar Veedhi, and since 1956 it has housed the principal bench of the Karnataka High Court. Its name means 'eighteen offices', recalling the reorganisation of Mysore's administration into eighteen departments in 1699. The building is a symmetrical two-storey block whose Ionic porticoes and arcaded linking wings form a distinctly European civic silhouette in an Indian setting.
landmarks.history: After Mysore's administration passed to a British Commission in 1831, ten secretariat departments operated out of Tipu Sultan's summer palace. Commissioner Lewin Bentham Bowring then conceived a dedicated secretariat building, and construction by Chief Engineer Richard Hieram Sankey ran from October 1864 to April 1868 at a total cost of Rs. 4,27,980, of which Rs. 3,68,981 covered construction and the balance acquiring and levelling the land. The building was known as the Old Public Offices Building and housed the secretariat, the Chief Court of Mysore and the Commissioner's office. Mysore administration returned to the Wadiyars in 1881 and the Legislative Council met on its third floor from 1907; an annex was added in 1917 and a major matching extension was completed in 1995 spanning 2,40,508 square feet. It was renamed the High Court of Mysore in 1929 and became the High Court of Karnataka in 1973. Demolition was approved by the Karnataka government on 24 March 1982 but was dropped in 1985 after the case reached the Supreme Court in B. V. Narayan Reddy v. State of Karnataka.
facts: Construction began in October 1864 and finished in April 1868; total cost was Rs. 4,27,980, of which Rs. 3,68,981 was construction.
Richard Hieram Sankey was the architect and Chief Engineer of Mysore State; the main contractor was Arcot Narainswamy Mudaliar; the building was conceived by Commissioner Lewin Bentham Bowring.
The name means 'eighteen offices', from the 1699 reorganisation of Mysore's administration into eighteen departments.
Each of the porticoes flanking the central wing has 12 Ionic columns; the main structure is enclosed on every side by porticoes and verandahs, with arcaded sections joining the wings.

Lower-storey walls are gneiss in chunam and upper-storey walls brick in chunam; the building is plastered and painted red ochre, with Grecian-style roof tiles. The foundation was 14 feet deep, built over former nullahs, and some of the stone slabs used were approximately 6-9 feet long.
An annex was added in 1917 and a major extension in 1995 spanning 2,40,508 sq ft, designed to match the original architectural style.

landmarks.name: Bangalore Palace
landmarks.description: Bangalore Palace, set on 454 acres in the Jayamahal area, is the seat of the Wodeyar dynasty and the most photographed building in the city. Its Tudor Revival design is explicitly modelled on Windsor Castle in England, giving the palace a fortified silhouette of towers, battlements and turreted parapets. The interior retains elaborate woodwork, a Durbar Hall with stained glass and carved ornament, and a ballroom with Victorian chandeliers and frescoes.
landmarks.history: The palace was commissioned by the Maharaja of Mysore for Chamarajendra Wadiyar X, with construction starting in 1873. Sources differ on completion: the infobox and history section give 1878, while the introduction states 1874. The site was formerly owned by John Garrett, a linguist and principal of Central High School, on whose land the palace was raised; the reported construction cost was ₹1 million. The Wodeyar family retained the palace as a residence and continues to use it for religious purposes, with the grounds and central courtyard now serving as a venue for concerts, exhibitions and weddings. The grounds also contain an amusement park and have been used as a film location.
facts: Construction began in 1873; the Wikipedia infobox lists 1878 as the completion year while the article introduction says 1874.
The palace stands on a plot of 454 acres (184 ha) formerly owned by John Garrett, a linguist and principal of Central High School.
The built-up area is listed as 45,000 sq ft (4,200 m²), with 34 rooms and a swimming pool.
Architectural style is Tudor Revival with the design based on Windsor Castle in England; sources describe a blend of Scottish and Gothic influences.

The Durbar Hall features intricate carvings, massive chandeliers and stained glass windows, and an elephant head adorns one wall; the Royal Gallery holds a collection of photographs documenting the Wodeyar dynasty.
Reported construction cost was ₹1 million, given a 2026 equivalent of ₹520 million (US$5.6 million).

landmarks.name: Bull Temple (Dodda Basavana Gudi / Basavanagudi Nandi Temple)
landmarks.description: The Bull Temple, better known as Dodda Basavana Gudi, is a compact Shaivite shrine in the Bugle Rock park at Basavanagudi in southern Bengaluru, whose monolithic granite Nandi bull is among the largest Nandi images in the world. Wikipedia places its construction in 1537 under the Vijayanagara Empire, crediting Kempe Gowda, the founder of Bengaluru, which makes it one of the oldest surviving temples in the city. The building itself is deliberately small - a shrine fronted by a porch, with a stepped vimana tower of the early 20th century carrying Saivite figures and motifs.
landmarks.history: The temple was built in 1537 by Kempe Gowda under the Vijayanagara Empire, in the same decade in which Kempe Gowda established the fortified Pete at Bengaluru, and it is listed among the early temples built or improved in the old city's suburbs. The main image is a large granite Nandi monolith, whose blackened surface is attributed to prolonged rubbing with charcoal and oil by generations of devotees; the image is continuously anointed with butter, called benne in Kannada, and a Ganesha image stands nearby. The temple hosts the Kadalekaayi Parishe, a groundnut fair held on the last Monday and Tuesday of the Hindu month of Karthika Maasa, when groundnuts are offered to the deity. The vimana over the shrine is a later addition dating from the early 20th century.
facts: Built in 1537 by Kempe Gowda under the Vijayanagara Empire; Wikipedia describes it as one of the oldest temples in Bengaluru.
The principal image is a large granite Nandi monolith approximately 15 ft (4.6 m) high and 20 ft (6.1 m) long, among the world's largest Nandi images.
The shrine is deliberately small, consisting only of the sanctum fronted by a porch; the vimana (tower) bearing Saivite figures and motifs dates from the early 20th century.
The blackened surface of the Nandi is attributed to prolonged rubbing with charcoal and oil, and the image is anointed daily with butter (benne).
The Kadalekaayi Parishe groundnut fair is held on the last Monday and Tuesday of the Hindu month Karthika Maasa, with groundnuts offered to the deity.
The temple stands on Bull Temple Road inside Bugle Rock Park in Basavanagudi, in southern Bengaluru; a Ganesha image stands in the same compound.

landmarks.name: Cubbon Park (Sri Chamarajendra Park)
landmarks.subcategory: Central urban park and museum precinct
landmarks.description: The central green lung of the Bengaluru CBD, officially Sri Chamarajendra Park, created in 1870 and now reported at 300 acres (1.2 km2). It weaves lawns and natural rock outcrops together with the Karnataka High Court, the Government Museum, the Seshadri Iyer Memorial Hall and its central library, a bandstand, a lotus pond and avenues of araucaria, ceal and gulmohar.
landmarks.history:
The park was created in 1870 and was first named Meade's Park after Sir John Meade, acting commissioner of Mysore; it was renamed Cubbon Park in 1873 after the longest-serving commissioner, Sir Mark Cubbon, and in 1927 renamed Sri Chamarajendra Park to commemorate the Silver Jubilee of Krishnaraja Wodeyar's rule. The original extent was 100 acres and the area is now reported at 300 acres (1.2 km2).

The buildings on the park's edges were laid out alongside it: the Attara Kacheri (1864), now the Karnataka High Court, the Government Museum (1876) and the Seshadri Iyer Memorial Hall (1915), which houses the central library. The equestrian statue of Sir Mark Cubbon was garlanded for the first time since independence on 23 August 2013, and on 28 June 2020 it was moved from the High Court premises into the park grounds.
facts: Created in 1870 as Meade's Park after Sir John Meade, renamed Cubbon Park in 1873 after Sir Mark Cubbon, and renamed Sri Chamarajendra Park in 1927.
The original area was 100 acres; the park's area is now reported to be 300 acres (1.2 km2).

Statues in the park include Queen Victoria (1906), King Edward VII (1919), Sir K. Sheshadri Iyer (1913) and Sri Chamarajendra Wodeyar (1927); the equestrian statue of Sir Mark Cubbon was moved into the park from the Karnataka High Court on 28 June 2020.
About 6,000 plants and trees of 68 genera and 96 species are recorded in the park.

The Seshadri Iyer Memorial Hall, built in 1915 in a classic European style with Tuscan and Corinthian columns, houses the central library with about 265,000 books; the library won the Raja Rammohan Roy award in 2000.

The park hosts the Bengaluru Aquarium, stated to be the second largest in India, and a toy train, the Putani Express, running 0.75 miles (1.2 km); roads around the park are closed to traffic from 5:00 to 8:00 a.m. for morning walkers.

landmarks.name: Gavi Gangadhareshwara Temple (Gavimath Cave Temple)
landmarks.description: The Gavi Gangadhareshwara Temple, or Gavimath (cave temple), is a Shaivite rock-cut shrine in Gavipuram, west of central Bengaluru, whose sanctum is hewn from monolithic stone inside a natural cave. The present temple was built or renovated by Kempe Gowda I, founder of Bengaluru, in the 16th century, and Wikipedia describes it as one of Bengaluru's oldest temples. Its defining feature is a solar alignment that allows sunlight to reach the inner lingam through the opening between the horns of the stone Nandi for about an hour around Makara Sankranti.
landmarks.history: The origins of the shrine are traditionally attributed to the Vedic-era sages Gautama Maharishi and Bharadwaja Muni; the present structure was built or renovated by Kempe Gowda I after his release from five years' imprisonment by Rama Raya. The complex was already being enlarged when Thomas and William Daniell painted it on 1 May 1792, and their drawings show subsequent additions including new walls and enclosures around the original cave. Today the alignment produces two annual illumination periods, roughly 13 to 16 January and 26 November to 2 December, when a shaft of sunlight falls through the gap between the Nandi's horns onto the inner lingam for about an hour, drawing large numbers of devotees; older Daniell drawings suggest that before the later additions the shrine was lit at the summer and winter solstices instead. The temple precinct also contains Gosaayi Math, the samadhi of Narayan Maharaj behind the shrine, and the Sri Bande Mahakali Temple. The site is protected under the Karnataka Ancient and Historical Monuments, Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1961.
facts: The sanctum is cut from monolithic stone within a natural cave at Gavipuram; the present temple was built or renovated by Kempe Gowda I in the 16th century.

Sunlight reaches the inner lingam through the opening between the horns of the stone Nandi for roughly an hour around Makara Sankranti; the present alignment produces two illumination windows, about 13-16 January and 26 November-2 December.
Comparisons with older Daniell drawings indicate that, before the later additions, the shrine was illuminated at the summer and winter solstices.

The courtyard holds numerous monolithic sculptures, including two granite pillars supporting a large disc representing the sun and moon, pillars carved with Nandi seated on top, and monolithic pillars associated with damaru and trishul imagery.

The complex includes shrines to Parvati, Ganesha, Murugan, Gautama Maharishi, Bharadwaja Muni, Chandikeswara, Durga, Agni, the Saptamatrikas, Dakshinamurthy, Bhairava, Veerabhadra, Lakshmi, Narayana, Surya, Chandra, the Navagrahas and others; the two-headed, seven-handed, three-legged Agni (Agnimurthi) is worshipped for the cure of eye defects.
Thomas and William Daniell painted the temple on 1 May 1792, and the site is protected under the Karnataka Ancient and Historical Monuments, Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1961.

landmarks.name: ISKCON Temple, Bengaluru (Sri Sri Radha Krishna Chandra Temple, Hare Krishna Hill)
landmarks.description: The ISKCON Temple on Hare Krishna Hill in Rajajinagar is described by Wikipedia as one of the largest Krishna-Hindu temples in the world, built by the International Society for Krishna Consciousness on a seven-acre hillock of monolithic rock allotted by the Bangalore Development Authority in 1988. Construction ran from 1990 to 1997 and the complex was inaugurated on 31 May 1997 by the ninth President of India, Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma. Its six shrines are housed in a hybrid design that the temple's own architects called "glass and gopuram" - traditional South Indian gopuram forms executed in carved granite and combined with modern glazing.
landmarks.history: ISKCON was founded in New York City in 1966 by Srila Prabhupada to promote the Bhagavad Gita and bhakti yoga; he was later posthumously honoured with the title Vishwa Guru by the Akhil Bharatiya Akhara Parishad at the Maha Kumbh Mela. The Bengaluru congregation first operated from a rented house in 1987 and petitioned the Bangalore Development Authority for land; on 3 August 1988 the BDA allotted a seven-acre hillock, largely monolithic rock unsuitable for building plots, called "karaab land". A temporary shed served as the first temple, and the deities of Sri Sri Krishna Balarama were installed there in September 1988 on Lord Balarama's appearance day. Construction began in 1990 and finished in 1997, when the temple was inaugurated by President Shankar Dayal Sharma; the original Rs. 10 crore plan was replaced by a Rs. 32 crore design. A second and larger complex has since been created on Vaikuntha Hill at Vasanthapura on Kanakapura Road, where the Rajadhiraja Govinda Temple was inaugurated on 14 June 2022 by President Ram Nath Kovind; Wikipedia describes the Vaikuntha Hills site as ISKCON's largest temple complex in the world, spread over 8 acres as a Krishna-lila theme park.
facts: Construction ran from 1990 to 1997 and the temple was inaugurated on 31 May 1997 by Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma, the ninth President of India.

The site is a seven-acre hillock of monolithic rock allotted by the Bangalore Development Authority on 3 August 1988; the deities of Sri Sri Krishna Balarama were installed in a temporary shed in September 1988, on Lord Balarama's appearance day.

The project grew from an original Rs. 10 crore plan to a Rs. 32 crore design, built by some 600 craftsmen contributing more than 10 million man-hours, using 32,000 cubic metres of stone, 131,250 tons of cement and 1,900 tons of steel.
Six shrines are dedicated: Radha-Krishna; Krishna-Balrama; Nitai Gauranga (Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Nityananda); Srinivasa Govinda (Venkateswara); Prahlada Narasimha; and Srila Prabhupada.
The gold-plated kalash shikhara measures 8.5 m (28 ft) and the gold-plated flag post (dhvaja) stands 17 m (56 ft) tall.
The design was conceived by civil engineer Madhu Pandit Dasa of IIT Mumbai with architect Sri Jagat Chandra Dasa, and is explicitly described by the temple as a fusion of "glass and gopuram".

landmarks.name: Kempegowda International Airport
landmarks.description: Kempegowda International Airport (KIA) is the airport serving Bengaluru, located at Devanahalli about 35 km north of the city centre at an elevation of 915 m. It has two passenger terminals: a domestic-only Terminal 1 and the much larger Terminal 2, which was designed as a tribute to the city's 'Garden City' identity by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and built by Larsen & Toubro. Two parallel 4,000 m x 45 m asphalt runways (09L/27R and 09R/27L) carry CAT IIIB instrument approaches, and the airport is described as Karnataka's first fully solar-powered airport.
landmarks.history: The airport opened on 24 May 2008, its first commercial arrival being Air India flight AI609 from Mumbai on 23 May, having been developed at an initial estimated cost of about 1,930 crore rupees. It was originally named Bengaluru International Airport; Karnataka proposed the Kempe Gowda name in February 2009, the Union accepted it in 2012, formal approval came in July 2013 and the official renaming took effect on 14 December 2013, when the expanded terminal was inaugurated. Terminal 2, designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and constructed by Larsen & Toubro at a cost of about 5,000 crore rupees, was inaugurated on 11 November 2022, began operations in January 2023 and took over all international flights on 12 September 2023.
facts: Opened 24 May 2008; first commercial arrival was Air India flight AI609 from Mumbai on 23 May 2008. Renamed Kempegowda International Airport on 14 December 2013, honouring the city's founder Kempe Gowda I.
Site elevation of 915 m, about 35 km north of central Bengaluru.
Terminal 1 has been domestic-only since September 2023, with a listed capacity of 35 million passengers a year, and was enlarged to 150,556 sq m.
Terminal 2 Phase 1 covers 255,000 sq m and adds 25 million passengers of annual capacity; a second phase is planned to add another 20 million.
Stated combined capacity of 55-60 million passengers a year after Terminal 2.
Two parallel asphalt runways, 09L/27R and 09R/27L, each 4,000 m long and 45 m wide, both with CAT IIIB instrument landing systems; the northern runway achieved full CAT IIIB capability in May 2025.
Costs: initial airport build about 1,930 crore rupees; first terminal expansion about 1,500 crore; broader second expansion about 4,000 crore; Terminal 2 Phase 1 about 5,000 crore rupees.
Karnataka's first fully solar-powered airport; the cargo village has space for nearly 80 trucks.

landmarks.name: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
landmarks.description: Bengaluru's best-known botanical garden, laid out on Mughal lines in the 1760s in the Mavalli area of south Bengaluru and organised around a lake fed by a chain of tanks. Its centrepiece is the 1889 cast-iron Glass House, set among lawns, topiary, rose and lotus gardens, and the 3,000-million-year-old Lalbagh Rock with a Kempe Gowda II watchtower above it.
landmarks.history:
Hyder Ali commissioned the garden in 1760 on the lines of the Mughal gardens at Sira, and his son Tipu Sultan completed it; the early gardens were managed by Mohammed Ali and his son Abdul Khader. After the British conquest of Mysore in 1799 the garden passed to Major Gilbert Waugh, then to the Mysore government in 1814, with Nathaniel Wallich supervising from 24 April 1819 and charge moving to the Mysore Commissioner in 1831. Hugh Cleghorn, appointed botanical advisor in 1855, recommended a European superintendent, and in August 1856 Lalbagh was made the Government Botanical Garden. William New arrived from Kew on 10 April 1858, followed by John Cameron, who directed the Glass House works, and after Cameron's retirement in 1908 by Gustav Herman Krumbiegel, after whom Krumbiegal Road is named.

The site expanded in stages: 45 acres in 1874, 30 acres added on the eastern side in 1889, 13 acres in 1891 including the rock with the Kempegowda tower, and 94 acres more in 1894, bringing the total to 188 acres. The Glass House foundation stone was laid on 30 November 1889 by Prince Albert Victor and the structure was extended in 1935 with steel from the Mysore Iron and Steel Company at Bhadravathi. Lalbagh, together with Cubbon Park, is protected by the Karnataka Government Park (Preservation) Act, 1975.
facts: Founded by Hyder Ali in 1760 on Mughal garden lines and completed by Tipu Sultan; the garden now covers 240 acres (0.97 km2).
Made the Government Botanical Garden in August 1856 on the advice of Hugh Cleghorn; the first Kew-trained superintendent, William New, arrived on 10 April 1858.

The Glass House, modelled on London's Crystal Palace, had its foundation stone laid on 30 November 1889 by Prince Albert Victor, was built with cast iron from the Saracen Foundry in Glasgow, and was extended in 1935 with steel from Mysore Iron and Steel Company at Bhadravathi.
A 15 ft high pigeon house or dovecote for 200 birds was built in 1893 south of the Glass House, and a central bandstand was added in 1890-91.
The Lalbagh Rock is 3,000-million-year-old peninsular gneiss designated a Geological Survey of India geological monument, with one of the four watchtowers of Kempe Gowda II above it.

The garden holds over 1,000 plant species with many trees more than a hundred years old, and stages flower shows in the week of 26 January and 15 August; the August 2022 Independence Day show was attended by 8.34 lakh people.

landmarks.name: Sree Kanteerava Stadium
landmarks.subcategory: Public sports complex and athletics stadium
landmarks.description: Bengaluru's largest sports complex, built on the bed of the drained Sampangi Lake and inaugurated in 1946 as Sampangi Stadium before being renamed for Yuvaraja Kanteerava Narasimharaja Wadiyar. Its eight-lane synthetic track and field-event surfaces were rebuilt for the 1997 National Games, and the arena still hosts football, athletics and rock climbing with the Cubbon Park tree line immediately to the south.
landmarks.history:
The stadium stands on the bed of the Sampangi Lake, which was perceived as an environmental hazard and was drained in 1937 after it had been neglected once piped water arrived from Hesaraghatta Lake within Bangalore. It was inaugurated in 1946 by Maharaja Jayachamaraja Wadiyar and named Sampangi Stadium after his father, Yuvaraja Kanteerava Narasimharaja Wadiyar, from whom it takes its present name. It originally had a six-lane cinder track; a synthetic running track was laid in the 1990s leading up to the 1997 National Games of India for INR 220 million, and was completed by 31 May 1997.

The stadium is owned by the Department of Youth Empowerment and Sports of the Government of Karnataka and is the largest sports complex in Bengaluru. The central arena consists of an eight-lane 400-metre synthetic athletic track with synthetic surfaced areas for shot put, discus, javelin, hammer throws, long jump, high jump, triple jump and pole vault; the ground also hosts walkathons, filmmaking, rallies and exhibitions, and contains a volleyball court and two outdoor rock-climbing walls. Four large arched entrances lead on to the inner field and lower stands, with eight ramps taking spectators to the upper stands, giving 12 spectator gates in total.

Sprinter Milkha Singh trained here in 1952; the stadium hosted the touring Soviet Union national team against a Mysore State XI in an exhibition match won 7-1, and the final of the 1962 Santosh Trophy won by the home Mysore team.

landmarks.name: St. Mary's Basilica, Bengaluru (Basilica of St. Mary, Blackpally)
landmarks.description: St. Mary's Basilica is the oldest surviving Catholic church of Bengaluru, a Gothic stone church in the Sampangi Rama Nagar / Shivajinagar quarter (historically Blackpally) whose twin spires rise about 49 m above the street. The present building, attributed to the Rev. L. E. Kleiner, was constructed between 1856 and 1882 and consecrated on 8 September 1882 by Bishop Jean-Yves-Marie Coadou. Pope Paul VI elevated it to the rank of Roman Catholic minor basilica in 1973, reportedly the sixth church in India to receive the title and the only one in Karnataka.
landmarks.history: The site began in the 17th century as a thatched shelter raised by Tamil Christian migrants from Gingee, called the Chapel of Kanikkai Madha, in the rice-growing settlement known as Bili Akki Palli or Blackpally. Fr. Jean-Antoine Dubois erected a thatched chapel there in 1803, added a small chapel and clergy residence in 1811, and in 1813 enlarged the building and renamed it the Church of the Purification of Our Lady. Fr. Andreas later expanded it into a cruciform plan, but it was destroyed during the communal riots of 1832. Its successor was built between 1856 and 1882 under the name Church of our Lady of the Presentation, and was consecrated on 8 September 1882 by Bishop Jean-Yves-Marie Coadou with 35 priests and roughly 4,000 Catholics present, at a reported cost of Rs. 29,659. The stained glass was taken out during the Second World War and restored in 1947. The church was elevated to minor-basilica rank by Pope Paul VI in 1973, and its principal feast, celebrating the Nativity of Mary, is held in September with a novena, multilingual Masses, thanksgiving services, Eucharistic observances and a concluding chariot procession that draws about 500,000 people.
facts: The present building was constructed between 1856 and 1882 and consecrated on 8 September 1882 by Bishop Jean-Yves-Marie Coadou, with 35 priests and about 4,000 Catholics present; the reported construction cost was Rs. 29,659.
The structure is attributed to the Rev. L. E. Kleiner and is Gothic in a cross-shaped plan, roughly 172 ft (52 m) long and 50 ft (15 m) wide, with two spires of nearly 160 ft (about 49 m).

The exterior is a grey-granite facade decorated with carvings and statues of biblical figures and scenes; the interior has vaulted ceilings on Corinthian pillars with pointed arches and detailed stained-glass windows.
The stained glass was removed during the Second World War and restored in 1947; a six-foot statue of Mary holding the infant Jesus stands outside and is traditionally dressed in a saree by devotees.

The church traces its origin to a 17th-century thatched 'Chapel of Kanikkai Madha' built by Tamil Christian migrants from Gingee; the church erected on that site was destroyed in the communal riots of 1832.
Pope Paul VI elevated it to a minor basilica in 1973, reportedly the sixth church in India to receive the designation; the September feast draws about 500,000 people.

landmarks.name: Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace
landmarks.description: Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace is a two-storey Indo-Islamic residence built entirely of teak inside the walls of Bangalore Fort, in the old quarters of Chamarajpet. Tall carved teak pillars on stone plinths carry heavy beams and support scalloped arches, bracketed balconies and durbar balconies on which Tipu Sultan held court. The structure stands on a raised rectangular stone base, and floral motifs adorn the ceilings and walls throughout.
landmarks.history: Hyder Ali began construction in 1781 within the fort walls, and his son Tipu Sultan completed the palace in 1791. Persian inscriptions on the building record the Hijri years 1196 (1781 AD) and 1206 (1791 AD). After Tipu Sultan's death in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, the British used the palace as their secretariat until 1868, when administration moved to Attara Kacheri. Tipu Sultan held durbar from the eastern and western upper-floor balconies, and four first-floor corner rooms served as Zenana quarters reserved for royal women. The building is listed as ASI monument N-KA-B2, "Tipu Sultan's Palace", in the Bangalore circle of centrally protected monuments. The Archaeological Survey of India now maintains the building, with the ground floor converted into a small museum.
facts: Construction ran 1781-1791, begun by Hyder Ali and completed by Tipu Sultan, with Persian inscriptions giving the years 1196 (1781 AD) and 1206 (1791 AD).

The ASI maintains the palace and the ground-floor rooms house a small museum of Tipu's achievements, portraits, clothing, crown and silver vessels, plus a replica of his Tiger (the original is said to be in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London).

landmarks.name: UB City
landmarks.subcategory: Mixed-use high-rise complex / luxury shopping mall
landmarks.description: UB City is a mixed-use high-rise complex on a 13-acre site at the corner of Kasturba Road and Vittal Mallya Road in the central business district, directly opposite Cubbon Park and 1.8 km from the MG Road-Brigade Road junction. It comprises six buildings with over 1.6 million sq ft of built-up area, combining the luxury retail mall 'The Collection', corporate offices (including United Breweries' own UB Tower) and service apartments. Its four towers are named Concorde (the UB Tower, 20 floors, 123 m to roof), Canberra, Comet and a fourth slab, giving the complex a stepped, clustered skyline.
landmarks.history: The development was established by the UB Group in a joint venture with the Prestige Group, with Prestige as main contractor, and construction began in 2004 with completion in 2008. The Times of India reported the project as 'finally here' in June 2006 while it was still being fitted out, and in June 2009 the Financial Express reported UB City winning an Asia-Pacific property award as a joint development venture between the two groups. The complex opened as India's first luxury shopping destination under the 'The Collection' banner, and UB Tower later gained an elevated rooftop helipad advertised as giving a five-minute aerial commute to Kempegowda International Airport.

landmarks.name: Ulsoor Lake
landmarks.subcategory: Urban lake with islands and a heritage bell tower
landmarks.description: One of Bengaluru's largest urban lakes, spread over 50 hectares (123.6 acres) east of the MG Road corridor, with four islands and a colonial watch tower that once held a Chinese bell. The shallow, silt-choked water body is shared between the Madras Engineer Group and BBMP and is now the subject of a desilting and sewage-diverting restoration programme.
landmarks.history:
The lake is traditionally dated to the time of the Kempe Gowdas, but its present form was created by Lewin Bentham Bowring, then Commissioner of Bangalore. Part of the lake is controlled by the Madras Engineer Group and the rest by BBMP. A study of the lake's ecosystem found a catchment area of 1.5 km2 fed by three drains - from the MEG Centre, from Jeevanahalli and from Doddigunta - the last traversing a chain of gardens and settlements, all within 1 km of the shore.

Restoration has included desilting, silt traps at stormwater inlets, diversion of sewage through 900 mm pipes, chain-link fencing and the reintroduction of fish and aquatic plants, along with improved training facilities for MEG boats. Public access runs from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and the lake is closed on Wednesdays. The eastern watch tower once carried a Chinese bell cast in 1741 under the Qianlong Emperor, whose cracked casting was later moved to the Madras Sappers Museum.

landmarks.name: Vidhana Soudha
landmarks.description: The Vidhana Soudha, standing on Ambedkar Veedhi on the High Grounds, is the seat of the Karnataka Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council. Its granite massing blends Dravidian and Indo-Saracenic elements, with Mysore Palace-inspired columns and a central dome carrying the Lion Capital of Ashoka. The building is among the largest granite structures in the world and Jawaharlal Nehru famously called it a 'temple dedicated to the nation'.
landmarks.history: The foundation stone was laid on 13 July 1951 and construction began in 1952, with the building completed and inaugurated in 1956. The design was by B. R. Manickam, who served as architect alongside chief engineer Muniappa, under principal supervisor Sir Arcot Narayanaswamy; the Karnataka Public Works Department was the main contractor. Granite was sourced from Magadi, Turuvekere, Mallasandra and Hesaraghatta, while door and window frames used principally Mysore teak. The central dome was sculpted by Siddalinga Swami and completed by his son Nagendra Stapati, with the Lion Capital emblem carved by Shilpi Shamachar. Interior wall paintings were executed by A. P. Rao in 1956. Reported costs differ between sources, from an original two-storey estimate of ₹33 lakh to a final cost of ₹1.8 crore for the redesigned building. In 2025 Karnataka introduced structured guided tours and opened designated interior areas to the public.
facts: The building measures approximately 700 feet north-south and 350 feet east-west, with a reported height of 46 m (150 ft) in the infobox and 53.34 m (175 ft) in the article body.
The east-facing entrance portico has 12 granite columns, each 12 m (40 ft) tall, approached by a flight of 45 steps that is 204 ft wide and 70 ft deep.
The central dome is 60 ft (18 m) in diameter, supported by 8 pillars and crowned with the Lion Capital of Ashoka; six smaller domes sit four in front and two behind.
The complex has 4 floors plus a basement, 172 rooms, and a total floor area reported as 550,505 sq ft (51,144 m²), with a plinth area of 132,600 sq ft.
The Legislative Assembly chamber measures 125 ft by 132 ft and is about 40 ft high, seating 254 with provision for 100 more; the Council chamber measures 100 ft by 78 ft and seats 88.
Two inner open quadrangles flank the central wing, which contains the Banquet Hall at ground level and the Assembly chamber above.

landmarks.name: World Trade Center Bengaluru
landmarks.description: The World Trade Center Bengaluru (WTCB) is a 32-storey, 128 m commercial tower in Malleshwaram West, near the ISKCON temple, Indian Institute of Science and Yeshvantpur Junction. Built by the Brigade Group under a World Trade Centers Association licence, it was the second World Trade Center in India after Mumbai and remains the tallest commercial building in Bengaluru. The tower sits inside the integrated Brigade Gateway enclave alongside Orion Mall, Manipal Hospital, the Sheraton hotel, a school and apartment blocks, with a skywalk bridge linking it to the Sheraton Grand Bangalore Hotel.
landmarks.history: The tower was opened for operation in 2010, reported by The Hindu in August 2010, having been built by Brigade Group after obtaining the World Trade Centers Association construction licence. At 128 m it was the tallest commercial building in South India from 2010 until 2015 and the tallest building in the city between 2010 and 2013. The surrounding Brigade Gateway development, which also contains Orion Mall, Manipal Hospital, the Sheraton hotel and the Brigade Gateway Apartments, received recognition in The Hindu's property review in January 2011.

landmarks.name: Anjaneya (Hanuman) Temple, Chickpet - Avenue Road crossing
landmarks.description: At the Avenue (Doddapete) road crossing in the old Pete stands an ancient Anjaneya - Hanuman - temple built by the Kempegowdas, the founders of Bengaluru, on the very square that formed the ceremonial heart of the original city. Wikipedia places it among the early temples built or improved under Kempegowda I (c. 1510-1570), alongside the Gavi Gangadhareshwara Temple, the Nandi (Bull) Temple, Dodda Ganapathi and Ulsoor Someswara. It is a modest neighbourhood shrine hemmed into the Chickpet bazaar frontage rather than a monumental temple, and it should be modelled at marker-plus level rather than with a full interior.
landmarks.history: Kempegowda I established the fortified Bengaluru Pete in 1537 with two main streets laid out in the cardinal directions: Chikkapet Street running east-west and Doddapet Street running north-south. Their intersection formed Doddapete Square - present-day Avenue Road - the heart of the old city, and it is at this crossing that the Anjaneya temple stands. The same Wikipedia account notes that the fort's northern extent ran from this Anjaneya temple, near Mysore Bank, south to Prof. Shivashankar Circle near Fort High School. The temple was among the early temples built or improved during the Kempegowda period, a group that also included the Gavi Gangadhareshwara Temple, Nandi (Basavanna), Dodda Ganapathi, Karanji Anjaneya, Ulsoor Someswara, Koramangala Lakshmi, Mahakali, Veerabhadra, Vinayaka and Kalabhairava. It is documented in photographs of the old Pete captioned "The ancient Hanuman temple built by Kempegowdas at the Avenue road crossing", and appears in Wikipedia's list of places of worship in Bengaluru.
facts: The temple stands at the Avenue (Doddapete) road crossing, where Chikkapet Street (east-west) and Doddapet Street (north-south) meet at Doddapete Square - today's Avenue Road, the heart of the old Pete.
The Bengaluru Pete was laid out by Kempegowda I in 1537, and the fort's northern boundary ran from this Anjaneya temple near Mysore Bank.

The shrine is documented in photographs of the old Pete captioned 'The ancient Hanuman temple built by Kempegowdas at the Avenue road crossing'.

It is a distinct, compact roadside shrine within the Chickpet bazaar district, separate from the Karanji Anjaneya and from the 16th-century Ranganathaswamy Temple a few hundred metres away on Chikkapet.
Its OSM/Photon record in the Bengaluru city dataset places it at approximately 12.9727 N, 77.5812 E, in the Chickpet quarter.

landmarks.name: Avenue Road (Doddaneedu Street)
landmarks.description: Avenue Road is a busy shopping and commercial street in Chickpet, central Bengaluru, linking Mysore Road with K. G. Road near Majestic bus station and Bangalore City railway station. Traditionally associated with used books, garments and textiles, jewellery and pawn brokering, it is the wholesale cloth centre of the old city and the main north-south axis of the Pete, running on toward Krishnarajendra Road.
landmarks.history: The street was earlier known as Doddapete - the name Doddaneedu is the Kannada form of the same word - and its name literally means 'Road Road'. It formed the Pete's principal north-south commercial axis, running from Mysore Road to Krishnarajendra Road and meeting the east-west Chikkapet Street at Doddapete Square; the Pete itself was founded in 1537 by Kempegowda I around a mud fort, with roads laid out to the cardinal directions and gates at their ends. Two illustrated views dated 1890 show the Canarese Chapel and the 'Main Street of the Pettah'. Rice Memorial Church still stands on the road, on the former grounds of the London Mission Canarese Chapel, established in 1834 by William Campbell, and commemorates Rev. Benjamin Holt Rice.

landmarks.name: Bangalore Fort
landmarks.description: Bangalore Fort was the fortified nucleus from which Kempe Gowda I created Bengaluru Pete in 1537, and it remains the anchor of the city's oldest quarter around Chamarajpet and Kalasipalya. A stone fortification with 26 towers and a broad ditch replaced the original earthwork in the eighteenth century, and the fort was Tipu Sultan's principal strongpoint before its fall to Lord Cornwallis in 1791. Almost nothing survives above ground but the Delhi Gate, two bastion remnants, and a marble plaque marking the British breach.
landmarks.history: Kempe Gowda I, a Vijayanagara chieftain, began construction of a mud fort in 1537 with nine large gates and a surrounding moat, and it was enlarged under Chikkadeva Raya Wodeyar during the seventeenth century. Hyder Ali replaced the old mud walls with stone; the Wikipedia infobox dates this stone phase to 1751 while the body text gives 1761. Tipu Sultan subsequently strengthened and repaired the defences and used the fort as a major stronghold. During the Third Mysore War in March 1791, the East India Company army under Lord Cornwallis besieged the fort, stormed the Pettah Gate on 7 March and breached the walls near the Delhi Gate, capturing the fort on 21 March 1791 after Mysore resistance that reportedly cost over 2,000 soldiers their lives. In November 2012 Metro construction workers uncovered two Tipu-era iron cannons, each weighing roughly one ton. The fort is listed as ASI monument N-KA-B1, "Old Dungeon Fort & Gates". The British then dismantled the defences, a process that continued into the 1930s, replacing ramparts with roads and barracks with hospitals, schools and colleges.
facts: Kempe Gowda I, a Vijayanagara vassal, began the mud fort in 1537 as the centre of Bengaluru Pete, with a moat and nine large gates.
Hyder Ali rebuilt it in stone - the Wikipedia infobox gives 1751 CE while the body text gives 1761.
A military description from around 1791 gives a stone fort perimeter of about one mile with 26 towers placed at intervals along the ramparts and a broad surrounding ditch.
Lord Cornwallis besieged the fort in March 1791 during the Third Mysore War; the Pettah Gate was stormed on 7 March 1791 and the fort was captured on 21 March 1791.
The British dismantling of the walls and ramparts continued until the 1930s; the fort area is now roughly one kilometre long, extending from the surviving gate toward the present KIMS campus.
All that remains above ground is the Delhi Gate and remnants of two bastions; a marble plaque marks the location of the wall breach.

landmarks.description: BIEC is a large exhibition and convention complex on the 10th Mile of Tumkur Road, developed and managed by the Indian Machine Tool Manufacturers' Association (IMTMA). Since opening it has hosted more than 400 events, including many national and international exhibitions.

landmarks.name: Bangalore University
landmarks.subcategory: Public university campus and central administration building
landmarks.description: Bangalore University is the public state university of Bengaluru, founded in 1964 as an offshoot of the University of Mysore and now based on the sprawling 1,100-acre Jnana Bharathi campus west of the city. Its administrative headquarters stands on Central College Avenue in the historic Central College building, formerly the Central High School founded by Rev. John Garrett in 1858. The institution retains 43 postgraduate departments and affiliates some 665 colleges across the region.
landmarks.history: The university was established in July 1964 as an offshoot of the University of Mysore covering the Bangalore, Kolar and Tumkur districts, with the nucleus formed by the Central College and the University Visvesvaraya College of Engineering. Honours courses were introduced in 1965-66. It operated from the Central College campus until moving to the new Jnana Bharathi campus in 1973, on about 1,100 acres; the University Law College (started 1948) and the College of Physical Education (started 1959) are both located there, along with the offices of the Vice-Chancellor and Registrar. The older Central College building, started as Central High School by Rev. John Garrett in 1858 and converted into a degree-awarding college in 1886, remains the university's city campus and houses offices, postgraduate departments, an auditorium and a cricket pavilion. Notable alumni include Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, C. N. R. Rao, Anil Kumble, Rahul Dravid and Sir M. Visvesvaraya. The university was awarded NAAC A++ accreditation in 2023, having earlier held Five Star status in 2001 and Grade A on reaccreditation in 2016.
facts: Established in July 1964 as an offshoot of the University of Mysore; the motto is 'Gyanam, Vignana Sahitam' (Knowledge along with Wisdom).

The nucleus was the Central College - begun as Central High School by Rev. John Garrett in 1858 and converted to a degree-awarding college in 1886 - together with the University Visvesvaraya College of Engineering, affiliated from 1964 to 2021.
The university moved into the Jnana Bharathi campus in 1973 on about 1,100 acres of land; a separate source gives the campus as 4.5 sq km.
It comprises six faculties - Arts, Science, Commerce & Management, Education, Law and Engineering - with 43 postgraduate departments and a postgraduate centre at Kolar begun in 1994-95.
It affiliates 665 colleges, of which 115 offer postgraduate courses; academic staff number 755 against a student body of 8,535.

NAAC accredited A++ in 2023, following Five Star status in 2001 and Grade A in 2016; ranked 551-600 in the QS Asian University Rankings 2023. A Karnataka government order of 1 July 2017 trifurcated the university into Bengaluru City University and Bengaluru North University.

landmarks.name: Bannerghatta National Park
landmarks.description: A 260.51 km2 national park in the Anekal hills about 22 km south of Bengaluru, declared in 1974, whose northern sector contains the Bannerghatta Biological Park zoo with its lion and tiger safari, snake park and butterfly park. Granite-sheeted ridges of moist deciduous forest valleys and scrubland are threaded by the Suvarnamukhi stream, and the park forms part of an elephant corridor linking the BR Hills to the Sathyamangalam forest.
landmarks.history:
The park was founded in 1970 and declared a national park in 1974; in 2002 a small portion of the park became the Bannerghatta Biological Park zoological garden. The 65,127.5-acre (260.51 km2) park lies about 22 km south of the city in the hills of the Anekal range at an elevation of 1,245 to 1,634 m, with hilly terrain of granite sheets under moist deciduous forest valleys and scrubland on the higher areas. Six rural villages sit within the park area in three large enclosures used for sheep and cattle farming, and sixteen villages border the park. Most of the park consists of artificial forest, and some animals have been introduced.

The park forms part of a wildlife corridor for elephants connecting the BR Hills and the Sathyamangalam forest, and is contiguous with Talli reserve forest in the south-east and Bilikal forest in the south. A guided bus tour runs along 6 km of safari roads made specially for safaris. Between 1995 and 2021 the park's dry deciduous forest shrank by approximately 44% because of uncontrolled diversion of forest land for agriculture and urbanisation, while granite quarries continue to operate inside the 1 km safe zone around the boundary.
facts: Founded in 1970 and declared a national park in 1974; in 2002 a small portion of the park became the Bannerghatta Biological Park zoological garden.
The park covers 65,127.5 acres (260.51 km2), lies about 22 km south of Bangalore in the hills of the Anekal range, and spans elevations of 1,245 to 1,634 m.
Six rural villages are enclosed within three large areas for sheep and cattle farming and sixteen villages border the park; a guided bus tour runs along 6 km of safari roads.
Rainfall is 700 mm per year and the Suvarnamukhi stream runs through the park; four borewells were opened on 15 May 2014 to provide water in dry times.

One hundred and one species of birds have been recorded, alongside Asian elephants, gaur, Indian boar, Indian leopard, sloth bears, Indian jackal, Bengal fox, dhole, sambar, chital, Indian pangolin, Indian python and king cobra.

Between 1995 and 2021 the dry deciduous forest shrank by approximately 44%; granite quarries operate within a 1 km safe zone around the boundary, with blast tremors felt across a radius of at least five km.

landmarks.name: Brigade Road
landmarks.description: Brigade Road is one of central Bengaluru's busiest retail districts, running north-south from M. G. Road down to Hosur Road with links en route to Residency Road and Church Street. It contains shopping centres, bookstores, international-brand stores, cafes, restaurants and pubs, and it is a long-established city celebration venue with fairy lights strung across the road for New Year.
landmarks.history: Brigade Road grew as the retail spine of the British-era central business district, and it retains several of its colonial and early-20th-century civic buildings - St. Patrick's Church, the Bengaluru Opera House and the Sapper War Memorial, the latter a First World War memorial to fallen members of the Madras Sappers & Miners (Madras Engineer Group). The Opera House was later leased to Samsung and rebranded as the Samsung Opera House, functioning as an experience centre and store. The street also became a marker of modern retail change: India's first KFC branch opened on Brigade Road in June 1995.

landmarks.name: Chickpet (Chickpete)
landmarks.description: Chickpet is one of Bengaluru's oldest commercial districts and the centre of the city's wholesale cloth trade. It occupies the eastern part of the old Pete, where the historic east-west axis of Chikkapet Street meets the north-south axis of Doddapet Street - today Avenue Road - at Doddapete Square. It has one of the smallest arterial roads in the entire city and is noted for the density of its marigold and jasmine garland sellers.
landmarks.history: Chickpet's roots go back to the 16th century. It is said that Shivaji spent his early childhood in Bengaluru with his father Shahaji Raje Bhosale, and that Shivaji's palace stood in the area now known as Chikkapete. Chickpet formed part of the Pete that Kempegowda I founded in 1537 around a mud fort, its principal east-west axis being Chikkapet Street. The district's commercial identity is textile: within the Pete it was historically associated with textiles, and the broader Pete traded in flowers, grain, bangles, oil, paper, stone and copper vessels by quarter. Chickpet retains the second largest Marwadi community in South India after Sowcarpet in Chennai.
facts: Chickpet's roots go back to the 16th century; Shivaji is said to have spent his childhood in Bengaluru with his father Shahaji Raje Bhosale, and his palace stood in the area now called Chikkapete.
It is one of the city's oldest areas and is famous for its cloth shops and wholesale businesses.
Chikkapet Street was the Pete's principal east-west axis; its junction with the north-south Doddapet Street became Doddapete Square, associated with today's Avenue Road.
The locality reportedly contains one of the smallest roads to serve as an arterial road in the entire city.
Chickpet has the second largest Marwadi community in South India, after Sowcarpet in Chennai.

landmarks.name: Christ University
landmarks.description: Christ University is a private deemed university in Bengaluru founded in 1969 as Christ College by the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate (CMI) congregation, granted UGC autonomy in 2004 and declared a deemed university in 2008. The flagship and main campus selected for this entry is the Bangalore Central Campus on Hosur Road, standing on 25 acres within the larger 100-acre Dharmaram Campus; the Bannerghatta Road campus at Hulimavu (opened May 2016) is a second, separate campus. The university runs a wide portfolio of UG, PG and doctoral programmes with 30,777 students, including about 700 international students from 58 nationalities.
landmarks.history: The institution traces its educational vision to St. Kuriakose Elias Chavara, who founded the CMI congregation in 1831, and was founded by the congregation in 1969 as Christ College on the Dharmaram campus. It received UGC autonomy in 2004 and deemed-university status in 2008; the chancellor is Rev. Dr. Saju Chackalackal. The Bannerghatta Road campus at Hulimavu was inaugurated in May 2016, and the university has since expanded to Kengeri (90 acres), Yeshwanthpur (1.6 million sq ft), Pune Lavasa (28 acres) and a Delhi NCR-Ghaziabad site (5 acres).

landmarks.name: Church Street
landmarks.description: Church Street is a 750-metre pedestrian-scale retail street in the central business district, running from Brigade Road to St. Mark's Road alongside M. G. Road. Named for St. Mark's Cathedral, which it leads to, it is a principal shopping and nightlife destination and a popular New Year's Eve gathering point. It was the first Bengaluru street to be paved with granite cobblestones and briefly became a motor-free pedestrian street.
landmarks.history: Church Street took its name from St. Mark's Cathedral, toward which the street leads. Redevelopment works costing 9 crore rupees began in 2017, laying granite cobblestones that made it the first Bengaluru street paved this way, in a 'Kasuti' arrangement intended to evoke Karnataka's cultural heritage. In 2020 the street was closed to motor vehicles under the 'Clean Air Street' trial, with outdoor seating, cultural programmes and buggies or e-rickshaws for disabled people and senior citizens; the trial ended on 31 May 2021. A bomb blast on the street on 14 May 2014 killed one person and injured four, with authorities suspecting the Indian Mujahideen.
facts: The street runs 750 metres from Brigade Road to St. Mark's Road alongside M G Road.
It is named for St. Mark's Cathedral, toward which the street leads.
2017 redevelopment works cost 9 crore rupees; the granite cobblestone 'Kasuti' paving made it the first Bengaluru street paved this way.

During the 2020 'Clean Air Street' trial, average daily footfall rose 92%, peak-period footfall rose 117%, more than half of establishments reported higher revenue, and 98% of surveyed users liked the pedestrianised street; the Indian Institute of Science monitored the trial.
The pedestrian trial ended on 31 May 2021; the stated reason was transfer to the BBMP, although the BBMP denied receiving instructions to continue.
An IED blast on the street in 2014 killed one person and injured four others, with authorities suspecting the Indian Mujahideen.

landmarks.name: Commercial Street
landmarks.description: Commercial Street is one of the oldest and busiest shopping areas of the city, running between OPH Road and K. Kamraj Road in the Tasker Town part of the central business district, with shopping continuing into bylanes such as Dispensary Road and Abrahim Sahab street. It trades in clothes, footwear, jewellery and electronics and is among the city's most crowded streets.
landmarks.history: Commercial Street sits inside the old Pete, the market core laid out by Kempegowda I in 1537 around a mud fort, with roads running to the cardinal directions and gates at their ends. The street's retail character dates from the colonial era, when the cantonment and the Pete markets were linked by a busy thoroughfare; photographs of the street survive from 1900 and from the Eid celebrations of 2012. The area's growth was never formally planned, and commerce has spread from the main carriageway into the surrounding bylanes.
facts: It runs between OPH Road and K. Kamraj Road, with associated shopping continuing into bylanes such as Dispensary Road and Abrahim Sahab street.
Wikipedia describes it as 'one of the oldest and busiest shopping areas of the city'.
Principal goods include clothes, footwear, jewellery and electronics, alongside numerous food establishments.
The street is among the city's most crowded, with only 75 four-wheeler parking spaces reported.
Archival photographs exist of Commercial Street in 1900 and during Eid in 2012.
It lies in the Shivajinagar / Tasker Town quarter of the central business district, near M G Road and Russell Market.

landmarks.name: Electronic City Phase 1
landmarks.description: Electronic City Phase 1 is the first and original phase of the KEONICS industrial township on the western side of Hosur Road in south Bengaluru, and today forms the 'Electronic City West' half of the estate. It is the campus district for the IT majors - OpenStreetMap tags the Infosys blocks by number (B25/26, B30/31, B32/33, B34/35/36/37, B38/39/40/41), alongside BHEL, Hewlett Packard GlobalSoft, NTTF, Fanuc and a Terminal Food Court. The township as a whole houses around 200 IT and ITES company campuses, with main campuses of Infosys, Wipro, TCS, HCL, Tech Mahindra and Biocon, and is served by the Yellow Line metro.
landmarks.history: Electronic City was the brainchild of R. K. Baliga (1929-1988), the first Chairman and Managing Director of KEONICS, Karnataka's electronics development corporation, who wanted to make Bengaluru the 'Silicon Valley of India'. KEONICS established the township in 1978 on 332 acres of land in the Konappana Agrahara and Doddathogur villages of Begur Hobli. Maintenance and upkeep passed to ELCITA, the Electronic City Township Industries Association, in 1997, and a notification of 18 March 2013 brought Phases I, II and III under the E-City Industrial Township Area. The estate grew to 903 acres and 11 guntas, with a further 122 acres acquired in 2003 to form Phase III, while Phase II covers about 340 acres.
facts: Phase 1 lies entirely on the western side of Hosur Road and forms 'Electronic City West'; the official township site places the estate at 12.85 N, 77.67 E on the Hosur Road (NH 7) corridor, about 9 km from Silk Board and 18 km from Vidhana Soudha.
Founded in 1978 on 332 acres in Konappana Agrahara and Doddathogur villages; the estate now covers 903 acres and 11 guntas over three phases.
Phase II covers about 340 acres and lies on both sides of Hosur Road; a further 122 acres acquired in 2003 formed Phase III.

Around 200 IT and ITES company campuses operate in Electronic City, including main campuses of Infosys, Wipro, TCS, HCL, Tech Mahindra and Biocon; major employers listed by Wikipedia include BHEL, Hewlett-Packard, Siemens, Continental, Genpact and Bosch.
A 9.985 km four-lane elevated expressway from Silk Board junction to Electronic City opened on 22 January 2010.

The 19.15 km elevated Yellow Line of Namma Metro (R.V. Road to Bommasandra, 16 stations) was inaugurated on 10 August 2025, with an Electronic City metro station, plus Konappana Agrahara station funded by the Infosys Foundation.
ELCITA, the township industries association, took over upkeep in 1997 and has deployed about 500 security officials with CCTV on strategic locations.

OpenStreetMap maps the Phase 1 Infosys campus in numbered blocks - B25/26, B30/31, B32/33, B34/35/36/37 and B38/39/40/41 - together with an Infosys fountain park, an Infosys skywalk, Hewlett Packard Avenue, the BHEL campus, NTTF and a Terminal Food Court.

landmarks.name: Government Museum, Bengaluru
landmarks.description: The Government Museum on Kasturba Road, beside Cubbon Park, is among the country's oldest museums and the second oldest archaeological museum in South India. Its red neoclassical building, designed by Col. Richard Hieram Sankey in 1877, has two porticos with Corinthian columns, round arches and prominent sloping parapet walls, and was popularly known as the tamasha house. Its 18 galleries on two exhibition floors hold the Halmidi inscription of 450 CE alongside Hoysala, Gandhara and Nolamba sculpture and excavated material from Mohenjodaro, Halebid and Vijayanagar.
landmarks.history: The museum was established on 18 August 1865 during Mysore State administration, following a Gazette notice on 17 April 1866, and was founded by Chief Commissioner L. B. Bowring under the guidance of Edward Green Berlephore. It first operated from a rented building, then in the Cantonment's jail building for 13 years until 1878. The purpose-built structure on what was then Sydney Road was planned and built in 1877, occupied in 1879, and the museum began functioning in it from 1880; the official Karnataka Archaeology Department gives 1877 as the year it was named the Mysore Government Museum and opened to the public. The building was designed by Col. Richard Hieram Sankey, then Chief Engineer of Mysore State. The museum closed temporarily for renovation for about a year as of a January 2024 report, with conservation carried out by KTIL at a cost of Rs. 540 lakhs.
facts: Established 18 August 1865, with the official Gazette notice following on 17 April 1866; founded by Chief Commissioner L. B. Bowring under the guidance of Edward Green Berlephore.

The present neoclassical building was designed by Col. Richard Hieram Sankey, Chief Engineer of Mysore State, and built in 1877 on what was then Sydney Road; it was occupied in 1879 and the museum functioned there from 1880.
Before this, the museum was first in a rented building and then in the Cantonment's jail building for 13 years until 1878.
Two exhibition floors are divided into 18 galleries covering sculpture, natural history, geology, art, music and numismatics.
The collection includes the Halmidi inscription of 450 CE, the Begur inscription of 890 CE and the Atakur slabs of 949 CE.

Holdings include sculpture from the Hoysala, Gandhara and Nolamba periods, and excavated artifacts from Mohenjodaro, Halebid and Vijayanagar - approximately 70 paintings and 84 sculptures. Average attendance was 280,000 in the 1870s and exceeded 400,000 in the early 20th century, against about 90,000 a year in more recent times.

landmarks.name: Hebbal Lake
landmarks.subcategory: Urban lake and bird habitat at the NH 7 / Outer Ring Road junction
landmarks.description: A shallow, predominantly eutrophic lake at the mouth of NH 7 where Bellary Road meets the Outer Ring Road, formed by bunding natural valley systems and now a magnet for water birds. Excavations and studies around its bund have also surfaced an 8th-century CE inscription recording a grant to a Durga idol, evidence of organised settlement and water management more than 1,200 years ago.
landmarks.history:
Hebbal Lake lies at the mouth of National Highway 7, along the junction of Bellary Road and the Outer Ring Road. It was formed by damming natural valley systems with bunds; the spread of the lake was measured at 75 ha in a 2000 study with plans to extend it to 143 ha, against an infobox area of 57 ha, and the article records 77.95 ha in 1974 and 57.75 ha in 1998. The Bhoopasandra inscription of the 8th century CE, found near the lake and studied by the historian and epigraphist Dr. P. V. Krishnamurthy, records a grant to a Durga idol originally located near the lake bund and mentions agrarian and water-management occupations, indicating organised settlement over 1,200 years ago.

The catchment of 3,750 ha includes Yeshwanthpur, Mathikere, Rajmahal Vilas Extension, BEL and HMT colonies, with an annual catchment of 15.2 million cubic metres and a storage capacity of 2.38 million cubic metres in 2000, raised to 4.07 million after desilting. Management was transferred to the Lake Development Authority in 2002; Indo-Norwegian Environment Programme funding of Rs 27 million from 1998 created two artificial islands from desilted soil as water-bird roosts, with desilting taken up in 2003. In 2004 the lake was leased for 15 years to East India Hotels (the Oberoi Group) at Rs 7,210,000 a year with 1.5% annual escalation, allowing a jetty, a gift centre and an island restaurant and the charging of entry fees.
facts: Formed by damming natural valley systems with bunds; a 2000 study found a 75 ha water spread with plans to extend it to 143 ha, the infobox area is 57 ha, and the recorded areas were 77.95 ha in 1974 and 57.75 ha in 1998.

An 8th-century CE Bhoopasandra inscription found near the lake records a grant to a Durga idol originally located near the lake bund, indicating organised settlement and water management over 1,200 years ago.

The catchment is 3,750 ha, the annual catchment is estimated at 15.2 million cubic metres (3.04 in the north-east monsoon, 10.12 in the south-west monsoon, 3.28 in the dry season), and storage capacity was 2.38 million cubic metres in 2000, rising to 4.07 million after desilting.

Management was transferred to the Lake Development Authority in 2002; Indo-Norwegian Environment Programme funding of Rs 27 million (US$700,000) from 1998 created two artificial islands from desilted soil as water-bird roosts, and desilting was taken up in 2003.

In 2004 the lake was leased for 15 years to East India Hotels (the Oberoi Group) at an annual lease of Rs 7,210,000 with 1.5% annual escalation, with a jetty, a handicraft and curio gift centre and an island restaurant permitted.

The lake is predominantly eutrophic with profuse water hyacinth and Typha in the shallow zone; in the late 1990s the weevils Neochetina bruchi and Neochetina eichhorniae were introduced from Argentina for biological control of the hyacinth.

landmarks.name: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore
landmarks.description: IIM Bangalore is the third Indian Institute of Management, established in 1973 and now an Institute of National Importance under the IIM Act 2017, with its 105-acre Bannerghatta Road campus in Bilekahalli. The campus was designed by B. V. Doshi as a 'poly-nuclear' plan of low blocks, passageways, pergolas and open quadrangles inspired by Fatehpur Sikri and the Meenakshi Temple, and its planting - 62 acres of green cover, about 30,000 trees and more than 50 groundwater recharge wells - was the founding director's way of expressing Bengaluru as 'green and alive'. The library occupies four levels and 55,000 sq ft, and the campus also hosts the 18,000 sq ft NSRCEL entrepreneurship centre.
landmarks.history: Design work began in 1977 with B. V. Doshi through his practice Stein, Doshi & Bhalla, assisted by Kanvinde & Rai, and original construction concluded in 1983. The poly-nuclear design combined Indian traditional planning with Team 10 modernist principles and was later placed among T magazine's 25 significant postwar works. The institute has since added a new classroom complex of about 6,500 sq m designed by Sanjay Mohe's Mindspace Architects, a 110-acre second campus near Jigani in Anekal Taluka about 20 km from the main campus, and a Management Development Centre at Jigani that opened on 1 March 2023; an IIMB station on the Namma Metro Pink Line was planned for March 2026.
facts: Established in 1973; the third IIM in the country, and an Institute of National Importance under the IIM Act 2017.
Main campus of about 105 acres (42 hectares) on Bannerghatta Road, with a second 110-acre campus near Jigani in Anekal Taluka about 20 km away.
Original academic complex of about 54,000 sq m; green cover of 62 acres with roughly 30,000 trees and more than 50 groundwater-recharge wells.

Central library of four levels and 55,000 sq ft, holding more than 163,000 printed books, 9,000 journals, over 42,000 periodical issues and access to more than 110 electronic databases; renovated 2016-19.
New Classroom Complex of about 6,500 sq m designed by Sanjay Mohe of Mindspace Architects; the NSRCEL building is 18,000 sq ft.
109 academic staff; the 2016 IIM Management Review is published quarterly through Elsevier; the IIMBx Open edX platform was launched in 2014.
Accredited by EFMD EQUIS since 2010; ranked second among Indian management institutes by NIRF in 2024 and 57th globally by the Financial Times for its MBA in 2025.
The campus also includes an academic block, a central pergola, an amphitheatre, a computer centre, hostel block L-Square and the library.

landmarks.history: JP Park, officially the Jayaprakash Narayan Biodiversity Park, occupies an 85-acre (340,000 m2) site at Mathikere in the north-west area of the city, beside Yeshwanthpur railway station. The park is organised around four lakes, with lawns spreading over about 25 acres (100,000 m2) and more than 250 varieties of trees and shrubs to be found there. Karnataka District Tourism describes the site with a lake, a musical fountain and paved walkways, and the BBMP list of Bengaluru lakes records J.P Park under the Mathikere ward of the Raja Rajeshwari Nagar zone. A running guide to the park describes a marked jogging circuit of about 1.8 to 1.9 km, with the Indian Institute of Science campus roughly 1.5 km to the west.
facts: The Jayaprakash Narayan Biodiversity Park covers an 85-acre (340,000 m2) site at Mathikere in the north-west of Bangalore, beside Yeshwanthpur railway station.

landmarks.name: KR Market (Krishnarajendra Market)
landmarks.description: Krishnarajendra Market - also called City Market - is the largest wholesale market dealing with commodities in Bengaluru, sitting in the Kalasipalya area beside Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace where Mysore Road meets Krishnarajendra Road. Fruit and vegetable stalls occupy the basement and lower ground floor of the main building, with flowers and dry goods above. It is also known as one of the biggest flower markets in Asia.
landmarks.history: The market was established in 1928 on a site that had earlier been a water tank and an 18th-century battlefield during the Anglo-Mysore Wars, and it was named after Krishnarajendra Wodeyar, a former ruler of the princely state of Mysore. The area is associated with Asia's first electric streetlights: Bengaluru lit them in August 1905, and Wikipedia's article on the market records it as the first locality in the whole of Asia to get electricity. Two British-era buildings survive on the site, one at the front and another at the rear; between them a three-storey concrete structure was built during the 1990s.
facts: The market was established in 1928 and named after Krishnarajendra Wodeyar, a former ruler of the princely state of Mysore.
Before the market, the site was reportedly a water tank and later an 18th-century battlefield during the Anglo-Mysore Wars.
It is described as the largest wholesale market dealing with commodities in Bangalore, and as one of the biggest flower markets in Asia.
Two British-era buildings survive, one at the front and another at the rear, with a three-storey concrete structure built between them in the 1990s.

landmarks.description: Mahatma Gandhi Road is the principal commercial spine of central Bengaluru, running east-west between Trinity Circle and Anil Kumble Circle past Cubbon Park, M. landmarks.name: Majestic (Kempegowda Bus Station)
landmarks.description: Majestic is the transport hub of Bengaluru, centred on the Kempegowda Bus Station opposite the KSR Bengaluru railway station. The at-grade complex handles both intercity KSRTC services and intracity BMTC buses, and is bounded by Seshadri Road, Danavanthri Road, Tank Bund Road and Gubbi Thotadappa Road. The Nadaprabhu Kempegowda, Majestic metro station on the Purple and Green lines sits directly above it.
landmarks.history: The bus station was first known as Majestic, after a nearby cinema theatre, and was later named for Kempe Gowda I; Majestic remains the most familiar name. Construction began in 1965 and the intercity station opened in 1969. The semicircular city-bus terminal was added in the 1980s, with the intracity section dated to 1980, and former Karnataka chief minister R. Gundu Rao is credited with developing the station. The site had formerly held Dharmambudhi Lake, which dried up in the early twentieth century. In 2025 Chief Minister Siddaramaiah announced redevelopment of the complex under the Project Majestic public-private-partnership scheme.

landmarks.name: Mayo Hall
landmarks.description: Mayo Hall is a two-storey memorial building on Mahatma Gandhi Road overlooking the Parade Grounds and Ulsoor Lake, raised in 1883 in memory of Richard Bourke, 6th Earl of Mayo, the fourth Viceroy of India. Its architecture mixes Greek cornices, Tuscan columns and keystoned arches with Italian chandeliers and ornate furniture, and it was the first public meeting and exhibition hall in the cantonment. The building now houses several departments of the Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike, with the Kempegowda Museum on the upper floor.
landmarks.history: Mayo Hall was inaugurated by the British Resident on 6 June 1883 at a cost of approximately Rs. 45,000, financed largely through public donations. It commemorates Richard Bourke, 6th Earl of Mayo, who served as Viceroy from 1869 to 1872, argued that Britain should retain control of India 'as long as the sun shines in heaven', and was killed by Sher Ali at the prison in Port Blair - the only Viceroy of India to be murdered while in office. The surrounding cantonment developed after the defeat of Tipu Sultan moved the British garrison from Seringapatam to Bengaluru in 1809. The ground floor was designed to accommodate the Cantonment Municipal Office, public offices and law courts, while the upper floor was intended for public meetings and exhibitions. A 2015 renovation changed the exterior from red-and-white to entirely red, and the Kempegowda Museum was established on the upper floor in 2011.

landmarks.name: Namma Metro - Nadaprabhu Kempegowda Station, Majestic
landmarks.subcategory: Rapid transit interchange (Purple and Green lines)
landmarks.description: Namma Metro is Bengaluru's rapid transit system, run by the Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited. The first section, between Baiyappanahalli and Peenya Industry, opened to the public on 20 October 2011, and the network is built around two corridors: the east-west Purple Line and the north-south Green Line. The two cross at Nadaprabhu Kempegowda Station, Majestic, an underground interchange within walking distance of the KSRTC Kempegowda Bus Station and the city's main railway station. Majestic is the busiest interchange in the city and the meeting point of the old bus-and-rail centre of gravity with the new one.
landmarks.history: Majestic station opened on 30 April 2016 as part of Phase 1. The contract to build it was awarded to Coastal-GTY JV at a cost of Rs 272 crore; construction began in January 2012 and was expected to finish by 2014, but the rock was hard to excavate, deadlines slipped and the cost escalated to about Rs 500 crore. KSRTC provided 20 acres of land for the works, slightly more than half of which was handed back afterwards, and BMRCL paid KSRTC Rs 4.6 crore a year in rent while construction went on. KSRTC lost about Rs 100 crore in the same period because bus services had to be suspended around the site. BMRCL employed 2,240 engineers, construction workers and others, and the underground stations of Phase 1 were built by cut-and-cover rather than tunnelling.

landmarks.name: Ranganathaswamy Temple, Bengaluru (Chikkapet / Chickpet)
landmarks.description: The Ranganathaswamy Temple stands on Rangaswamy Temple Road in Chikkapet (Chickpet), the old trading heart of Bengaluru, and is a 16th-century Vaikhanasa Vaishnava temple built under the Vijayanagara Empire. It is named for Ranganatha, the reclining form of Vishnu, and the surrounding road took its name from the shrine. The temple follows Vijayanagara architecture with carved granite pillars showing Hoysala influence, and encloses its sanctum within an inner praakaara so that devotees can circle it.
landmarks.history: The temple dates to the 16th century CE, the period when the Vijayanagara Empire dominated the Deccan and Kempe Gowda's new city was being established on the site of the old Pete; it became the spiritual anchor of the Chickpet bazaar, whose streets - Chikkapet Street and Doddapet Street - were laid out in 1537. Wikipedia records the surrounding road as named after the temple, and lists it among the ancient and famous Vaikhanasa temples of the city. Worship follows the Vaikhanasa Agama: the Rathotsavam, the temple's chariot festival, falls on Chaitra Shuddha Pournami and is held on the same day as the Bangalore Karaga festival, when the moolavar and utsavar murtis are taken out; and during Vaikuntha Ekadashi devotees perform pradakshina within the inner enclosure, with special darshan of both the main and processional deities.

landmarks.name: Sankey Tank
landmarks.subcategory: Historic reservoir converted into a public park
landmarks.description: An 1882 drinking-water reservoir built by Colonel Richard Hieram Sankey of the Madras Sappers Regiment, formerly called Gandhadhakotikere, now landscaped as a public park between Malleshwaram, Vyalikaval and Sadashivanagar. The 15-hectare tank holds a single island and a 1.7 km shoreline, and its wooded bund, nursery and paved walks make it one of the most used neighbourhood parks in the city.
landmarks.history:
Sankey Tank was constructed in 1882 to meet the water-supply demands of Bangalore. It was linked to the Miller's Tank and the Dharmambudhi Tank and was built as a safeguard against the water shortages experienced during the Great Famine of 1876-78. The quality of the water was poor: when the Governor of Madras visited Bangalore in July 1888 a local wit remarked that the men killed on the spot at Bangalore were the only ones doctors did not allow to die of drinking bad water. Seven sewage inflow points were later identified.

In the early 2000s the tank was developed into a park by BWSSB and BBMP with Karnataka government funding, with measures including removing encroachments, alum purification, a nursery to the north, paved walkways, landscaped parks, a special idol-immersion tank for Ganesh Chaturthi and restoration of a swimming pool. Development pressure followed: in 2004 a Karnataka Lok Adalat ordered the Forest Department to repossess 0.52 ha (1.3 acres) from developers, the LDA recommended a 100 m no-construction buffer, and an 18-floor apartment proposal was turned down by the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board.

Covers about 15 ha (37.1 acres), is 800 m at its widest, has a maximum depth of 9.26 m, a shoreline of 1.7 km, a catchment of 1.254 km2, a surface elevation of 929.8 m and one island.

Converted into a public park in the early 2000s by BWSSB and BBMP with Karnataka government funding; the works included removing encroachments, alum purification, a nursery to the north, paved walkways, landscaped parks, a special idol-immersion tank for Ganesh Chaturthi and restoration of a swimming pool.

In 2004 a Karnataka Lok Adalat ordered the Forest Department to repossess 0.52 ha (1.3 acres) from developers, the LDA recommended a 100 m no-construction buffer, and an 18-floor apartment proposal was turned down by the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board.
Seven sewage inflow points were identified; 2001 tests measured dissolved oxygen of 3.7-8.1 mg/L, BOD of 2-8 mg/L and pH of 7.1-7.5.

landmarks.name: Sri Govardhanagiri Kshetra (Krishna Temple), Basavanagudi
landmarks.subcategory: Hindu temple (Krishna shrine, artificial cave temple, Puttige Matha)
landmarks.description: The one genuine Krishna temple inside the Bengaluru city boundary that can be documented with a full street address is the Sri Govardhanagiri Kshetra at 1/3 Bull Temple Road, opposite BMS Engineering College, Basavanagudi. It is an artificial cave temple carved into and around a pre-existing hill, whose central shrine holds Krishna as Govardhana Giridhari, lifting Govardhana hill on his little finger; it was inaugurated on 4 March 2004 by Sri Sugunendra Teertha Swamiji, the 30th Peetathipati of the Puttige Matha of Udupi, and dedicated by Dr. Nalini Rao. Note on the brief: the famous "Krishna Temple, Udupi" (Sri Krishna Matha, Madhvacharya's 13th-century Dvaita matha) lies about 400 km north-west of Bengaluru, outside the metro area, and is not modelled here; this entry instead uses the in-city Krishna shrine, which is administered by that same Udupi matha tradition.
landmarks.history: The temple was inaugurated on 4 March 2004 by Sri Sugunendra Teertha Swamiji, the 30th Peetathipati of the Puttige Matha, Udupi, and was dedicated by Dr. Nalini Rao in memory of her parents and brother. The design is a unique artificial cave temple built around a pre-existing hill, so that the exterior imitates Govardhanagiri itself: the entrance leads through a dim tunnel with stone shoe racks and wheelchair access into the sanctum, and the wall friezes depict episodes from Krishna Leela. The precinct includes gardens, a goshala with two cows offering Go-Seva, a Prashadalaya, a Puthige Mutt branch and function halls, and the site is affiliated to the Puttige Matha, Udupi, following the Madhwa tradition. A separate smaller Ganesha shrine is listed at the site alongside the central Krishna shrine.
