landmarks.name: St. Mary's Jacobite Syriac Orthodox Cathedral, Bengaluru (Queen's Road, Vasanth Nagar)
landmarks.description: The only building in Bengaluru that is styled "St. Mary's Cathedral" is the St. Mary's Jacobite Syriac Orthodox Church on Queen's Road, Vasanth Nagar, the cathedral church of the Jacobite Syriac Orthodox Church's Bangalore Diocese; it is listed among India's Jacobite Syriac cathedrals in Wikipedia. The congregation was founded in 1975 by Malayali Syriac Christian migrants - Syriac worship in the city dates from 1936 - and the present church grew from a trust formed in 1978 on land leased from the Bangalore city corporation. Important correction to the brief: there is no 1880s Gothic Revival cathedral on MG Road in Bengaluru; MG Road's cathedral is St. Mark's Cathedral (foundation 1808, consecrated 1816, English Baroque) and the Gothic church of 1875-1882 is St. Mary's Basilica in Shivajinagar, recorded separately as st-marys-basilica.
landmarks.history: Syrian Christian worship began in Bengaluru in 1936 with the arrival of Malayali Christians. In 1975, after a church conflict, a congregation on Queen's Road was formed and first gathered with about 200 members, holding its first Mass with the Rev. Fr. P.V. Paolose of Kolancherry, Ernakulam; the Rev. Fr. George Jacob and the Rev. Fr. K.M. Paulose served as vicars through 1976. In June 1976 the Rev. Fr. M.K. Thomas - later identified as H.G. Thomas Mor Themothoes, Metropolitan - became vicar, and Sunday worship moved from the Bangalore Lutheran Church to United Theological College, Bengaluru. To establish a legal body a trust named St. Mary's Jacobite Society was formed in 1978, after which the congregation obtained a leased plot from the Bangalore city corporation and raised the present cathedral church on it. The cathedral's own published history notes no construction or consecration dates, so the building's date should be treated as post-1978 and unconfirmed.
facts: The congregation was founded in 1975 with about 200 members; the first Mass was celebrated by the Rev. Fr. P.V. Paolose of Kolancherry, Ernakulam, and the Rev. Fr. George Jacob and Rev. Fr. K.M. Paulose served as vicars through 1976.

The Rev. Fr. M.K. Thomas - later H.G. Thomas Mor Themothoes, Metropolitan - became vicar in June 1976, and Sunday worship then moved from the Bangalore Lutheran Church to United Theological College, Bengaluru.
A trust named St. Mary's Jacobite Society was formed in 1978, and the congregation subsequently obtained a leased plot from the Bangalore city corporation on which the cathedral church was built.

landmarks.name: Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum
landmarks.description: The Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum, founded in memory of Sir M. Visvesvaraya, is a modest modernist pavilion of 4,000 sq m on the edge of Cubbon Park on Kasturba Road. It was inaugurated by Jawaharlal Nehru on 14 July 1962 and houses an unusually broad set of working exhibits - engines, electronics, space technology, biotechnology, a dinosaur enclave and the Wright Brothers' aeroplane - rather than static cases. A 1979 extension raised its total area to 6,900 sq m.
landmarks.history: The All India Manufacturers Organization and the Mysore State Board decided to create a science and technology museum in Bangalore in memory of Sir M. Visvesvaraya, and Shri B. D. Jatti, then Chief Minister of Mysore, laid the foundation stone on 15 September 1958. The museum opened on 14 July 1962, inaugurated by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. The museum treats 27 July 1965 - when the ElectroTechnic gallery was opened to the public by Indira Gandhi - as its foundation day. A mobile exhibition began in 1970 with 24 participatory exhibits, and NCSM was registered on 4 April 1978. A 1979 extension brought the total floor area to 6,900 sq m. The museum is a unit of the National Council of Science Museums under India's Ministry of Culture; the adjoining Jawaharlal Nehru Planetarium, established in 1989 on Sri T. Choudaiah Road, High Grounds with its own outdoor Science Park, is a separate institution. The Fun Science Gallery opened on 27 July 2025, and a mirror maze in the Science for Kids gallery was inaugurated on 19 April 2019.
facts: Opened on 14 July 1962 and inaugurated by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru; the foundation stone was laid by Shri B. D. Jatti, then Chief Minister of Mysore, on 15 September 1958.
The original Cubbon Park building had a built-up area of 4,000 sq m (43,000 sq ft); a 1979 extension raised the total to 6,900 sq m (74,000 sq ft).

Galleries include the Engine Hall, ElectroTechnic, Fun Science, Space Technology, Biotechnology, BEL Hall of Electronics, Dinosaur Enclave, Wright Brothers' Aeroplane, Science on a Sphere, 3D Show, Science Park, Seed of Culture and Mars Rover Opportunity.
The museum displays industrial products, scientific models and engines, and also hosts science demonstrations, sky observation and popular-science lectures.
A mirror maze in the Science for Kids gallery was inaugurated on 19 April 2019; the Fun Science Gallery opened on 27 July 2025.
A Collaborative Multi-Layer 3D Display System was launched in the BEL Hall of Electronics, third floor, on 13 March 2026. The museum's own site reports more than 10.5 million visitors in total.

landmarks.name: Bannerghatta Road (Karnataka State Highway 87)
landmarks.description: Bannerghatta Road is Karnataka State Highway 87, the main arterial running south from the Hosur Road junction at Adugodi through Bilekahalli, Arekere, Hulimavu and Gottigere to Jigani and Anekal at the Tamil Nadu border. It is the spine of south Bengaluru, carrying the IIM Bangalore campus and Christ University's Hulimavu campus, the Jayadeva, Apollo, Fortis and Narayana hospitals, and the Vega City, Royal Meenakshi, Shoppers Stop and Gopalan mall cluster, with the Namma Metro Pink Line running along it to IIMB. The corridor carries the elevated NICE expressway interchange near Gottigere and the Bangalore-Mysore Infrastructure Corridor crossing.
landmarks.history: The highway was originally laid as the road from Bangalore to Bannerghatta, then extended through Jigani to Anekal and on to Samanduru at the Tamil Nadu state boundary, where it continues as a Major District Road and merges with National Highway 948 A. In 2011 the Bruhat Bangalore Mahanagara Palike announced selective widening of the road from 20-25 metres to 45 metres together with underpasses and flyovers at major junctions, at an estimated cost of 137 crore rupees. Grade separation followed with the Dairy Circle and Jayadeva underpasses, and for about five kilometres south of the Jayadeva Underpass the road was widened to four lanes by Mantri Developers in one of Bengaluru's earliest public-private partnership infrastructure projects. The Pink Line of the Namma Metro was then routed along the corridor, from Kalena Agrahara to Nagawara via IIMB, to take traffic off the road.

Length given as 45 km in the article text and 49 km in the infobox.

Two grade-separated underpasses exist on the corridor: the Dairy Circle Underpass and the Jayadeva Underpass; a flyover sits at Dairy Circle.
About five kilometres south of the Jayadeva Underpass the road was widened to four lanes by Mantri Developers under one of Bengaluru's earliest public-private partnerships.
Major intersections: Hosur Road at Adugodi, Marigowda Road at Dairy Circle, Marenahalli Road and the Outer Ring Road at the Jayadeva Hospital interchange, and the NICE corridor near Gottigere.
The Outer Ring Road runs concurrently with Bannerghatta Road from the Jayadeva Hospital Interchange to JD Mara Junction in front of Vega City Mall before diverging towards Electronic City.

Institutions on the corridor include IIM Bangalore (between Bilekahalli and Arekere) and Christ University's Dairy Circle and Hulimavu campuses; hospitals include Sri Jayadeva Institute, Apollo, Fortis and Narayana Health; malls include Gopalan Innovation Mall, Shoppers Stop, Vega City and Royal Meenakshi Mall.
The Namma Metro Pink Line runs from Kalena Agrahara to Nagawara along the corridor via IIMB.
Note for modellers: the current National Highway 12 runs entirely within West Bengal and does not include this corridor - Bannerghatta Road is a state highway, not an NH 12 route.

landmarks.name: Basavanagudi
landmarks.description: Basavanagudi is a residential and commercial locality in south Bengaluru, named after the Bull Temple whose monolithic Nandi gives the place its name - 'basava' means bull and 'gudi' means temple in Kannada. DVG Road runs through it as the neighbourhood's commercial spine, and midway along that road the Gandhi Bazaar market opens into a dense lane of flower, fruit and vegetable stalls. The locality also holds B.M.S. College of Engineering and the century-old Vidyarthi Bhavan restaurant.
landmarks.history: Basavanagudi is described as one of the oldest and 'poshest' localities of Bangalore, a status evidenced by four inscriptions in the neighbourhood, three in Kannada and one in Tamil, and by the 1537 Bull Temple built by Kempe Gowda during the Vijayanagara Empire. Development was guided by the same 1889 K. Seshadri Iyer committee that planned Malleswaram, which laid out Basavanagudi in the same period as a residential quarter south of the old Pete. The commercial spine grew along DVG Road, where several of the retail businesses date back to the 1920s and 1930s; Vidyarthi Bhavan, the neighbourhood's best-known vegetarian restaurant, opened in 1943, and B.M.S. College of Engineering was established in 1946.
facts: The Bull Temple was built in 1537 by Kempe Gowda in Vijayanagara style; its present vimana was added in the early 20th century and decorated with Saivite figures and motifs.

The temple's monolithic granite Nandi stands on a plinth, blackened by repeated applications of charcoal and oil, and measures about 15 ft (4.6 m) high and 20 ft (6.1 m) long - among the world's largest Nandi images.
The locality is home to four inscriptions, three in Kannada and one in Tamil.
B.M.S. College of Engineering was established in 1946 and is credited as the first private engineering college in India.
Vidyarthi Bhavan, the vegetarian restaurant on the DVG Road, opened in 1943.
Wikipedia's locality infobox records a population of 32,640 for the Census of 2011; PIN codes are 560004, 560019, 560028 and 560050.

landmarks.name: Gandhi Bazaar
landmarks.description: Gandhi Bazaar is a traditional street market midway along DVG Road in Basavanagudi, and one of Bengaluru's oldest trading areas. It is known for flower, condiment, fruit, vegetable and cloth stalls and for its old eating houses, and it swells with crowds at festivals when shoppers buy puja items. The Kannada writer Masti Venkatesha Iyengar lived here.
landmarks.history: Gandhi Bazaar sits in the heart of Basavanagudi, the residential quarter laid out in the 1880s by the K. Seshadri Iyer committee alongside Malleswaram. DVG Road, which runs through the bazaar, forms Basavanagudi's commercial centre and contains some of the city's oldest business outlets, several dating back to the 1920s and 1930s. The bazaar's character as a conservative, traditional market quarter was reinforced by the presence of long-standing residents such as Masti Venkatesha Iyengar, and by the century-old vegetarian restaurant Vidyarthi Bhavan, which opened in 1943 nearby.

landmarks.name: Indiranagar
landmarks.description: Indiranagar is an east-central locality that began as a bungalow suburb and became one of Bengaluru's most commercialised districts after the IT boom. Its two spine corridors - 100 Feet Road and CMH Hospital Road - carry high-end fashion stores, bars and pubs, while the side streets remain a low-rise residential quarter of independent houses.
landmarks.history: Indiranagar was formed as a Bangalore Development Authority layout in the late 1970s and was named after M. K. Indira. It started as a suburb of bungalows and detached houses and became more commercial after Bengaluru's late-1990s IT boom; it is now both an important residential and a commercial hub. 100 Feet Road and CMH Hospital Road became the commercial corridors, with BMTC bus routes running along CMH Road, 80 Feet Road and 100 Feet Road and 12th Main Road serving the 100 Feet Road corridor. The Purple Line of the Namma Metro serves the area through the Indiranagar and Swami Vivekananda Road stations.

landmarks.name: Jamia Masjid, Bengaluru (City Market)
landmarks.description: The Jamia Masjid near the City Market is the most impressive mosque in Bengaluru. Designed by Rayyaz Asifuddin of Hyderabad, it was built in 1940 with white marble from Rajasthan and is dedicated to Tipu Sultan. The building has bulbous domes, twin towers standing on exquisitely carved granite pillars, and jali work in the balcony. It is a five-storeyed structure with space for up to 10,000 devotees, and an ablution pool at its centre. It stands in the heart of the Pete, the old market city that has been the centre of Bengaluru's Muslim trading community for centuries.
landmarks.history: The earliest recorded history of Islamic influence in Bengaluru goes back to 1638, when the old Pete was taken by the Bijapur Sultanate, who ruled for the next fifty years. The Mughal general Khasim Khan captured the town in 1687, and in 1690 leased it and the surrounding areas to Chikkadeva Raya Wodeyar of the Kingdom of Mysore. Hyder Ali became Sarvadhikari of Bangalore in 1761, and the Mysore Sultanate that followed - from 1761 until Tipu Sultan was killed in 1799 - saw many mosques and dargahs built. Over the 370 years from the Bijapur conquest, more than 400 Muslim shrines were established in the city. The Jamia Masjid itself was completed in 1940, in the final years of British rule.

landmarks.name: Jayanagar
landmarks.description: Jayanagar is south Bengaluru's flagship planned neighbourhood, laid out in 1948 on the model of New Delhi and divided into ten numbered blocks. Its Kannada name combines 'Jaya' and 'nagar' - literally 'Victory City'. Most blocks are residential villas and apartment blocks, while the 3rd and 4th Blocks are the commercial core, home of the Jayanagar Shopping Complex and the district's busiest market street.
landmarks.history: The foundation of Jayanagar was laid in 1948, making it one of Bengaluru's earliest planned neighbourhoods and, at the time, one of the largest in Asia. Before the city's expansion, Jayanagar marked the southern limit of the urban area - the historic South End Circle and the Ashoka Pillar were the boundary markers, with 'South End' still used for the district. The layout was divided into ten blocks numbered 1 to 9 plus a fourth 'T' block, and it was later divided into seven wards. The Jayanagar BDA Shopping Complex opened in 1976 with the Puttanna Kanagal theatre inside; a fire in 2008 damaged it, and redevelopment beginning around 2011-12, at a cost of roughly 193 crore rupees, included demolishing the theatre.

The locality comprises seven wards and had about 180,000 voters in 2013.

landmarks.description: Jayanagar 4th Block is the principal commercial block of Jayanagar, centred on the Jayanagar Shopping Complex and its surrounding street market. It serves as the shopping district for the whole of south Bengaluru, with clothing, footwear, bags, jewellery and food stalls strung along the main cross. The Green Line Jayanagar metro station serves the 4th and 7th Blocks.
landmarks.history: The block was laid out with the rest of Jayanagar when the neighbourhood was planned in 1948, but became the district's commercial centre with the opening of the Jayanagar BDA Shopping Complex in 1976, which contained the Puttanna Kanagal theatre. A fire in 2008 damaged the complex; redevelopment beginning around 2011-12, at a cost of roughly 193 crore rupees, included demolishing the theatre. The 3rd and 4th Blocks remain the two principally commercial blocks of the locality, while the other blocks are residential.

landmarks.name: Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath
landmarks.subcategory: Fine arts academy and gallery complex
landmarks.description: The Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath is the state's premier fine arts academy, occupying a three-acre wooded compound on Kumara Krupa Road beside the Chief Minister's residence. Founded in 1960 by artists including S. S. Kukke, M. Arya Murthy and M. S. Nanjunda Rao, it now runs the College of Fine Arts and 18 galleries of permanent painting, sculpture and folk art collections. The surrounding neighbourhood hosts the annual Chitra Santhe open-air art fair.
landmarks.history: The organisation began in 1960 as the Mysore Chitrakala Parishath, founded by S. S. Kukke, M. Arya Murthy and M. S. Nanjunda Rao, starting in Aryamurthy's garage in Shantinagar in 1960 and moving to the upper floor of Gandhi Sahitya Sangha, Malleswaram, from 1964. In 1964 it also became the arts college Chitrakala Vidyalaya, later the College of Fine Arts, with diploma courses taught by M. S. Nanjunda Rao, M. Gopal and S. S. Kukke, gaining state and Lalit Kala Akademi recognition in 1966. The institution relocated to its present Kumara Krupa Road site in the mid-1970s, on three acres of thicket leased from the Karnataka government next to the Chief Minister's bungalow. It presents the Chitrakala Samman award to four senior artists, and its collection includes 36 Nicholas Roerich paintings donated by Svetoslav Roerich.
facts: Founded in 1960 by S. S. Kukke, M. Arya Murthy and M. S. Nanjunda Rao, initially in Aryamurthy's garage in Shantinagar.

The folk-art display includes Mysore paintings and leather puppets, and the collection holds 36 Nicholas Roerich paintings donated by Svetoslav Roerich.
The Chitra Santhe art fair has been held annually since 2004 on the last Sunday of January, turning the road from Shivananda Circle to Windsor Manor into an open gallery from 8 am to 8 pm.

landmarks.name: Kempegowda Circle (Gavigangadeshwara Temple and the Pete)
landmarks.description: Kempegowda Circle is the crowded junction at the heart of the old Pete, and the place where Bengaluru's founder is commemorated: a statue of Kempegowda stands at the centre of the circle, with the Gavigangadeshwara Temple beside it and the Kempegowda Tower on the circle's edge. Kempegowda I, a governor of the Vijayanagara Empire, laid out the Pete here in 1537 with roads running in the cardinal directions and entrance gates at the end of each road, and called it his 'gandu bhoomi', the land of heroes. The market city that grew around that plan - Tharagupete for grain, Balepete for bangles and musical instruments, Chikkapete and Nagarthpete for textiles, Ballapurpete and Ganigarapete for oil, Tigalarapete for flowers, Cubbonpete for cloth made by the Devanga community - is still the commercial heart of the city.
landmarks.history: The Pete was established by Kempe Gowda I in 1537 around the mud fort he built as its nucleus, with roads laid out in the cardinal directions and entrance gates at the end of each road. He also termed it his 'gandu bhoomi', or land of heroes. The area covered about 2.24 square kilometres and has since been absorbed into a metropolis of roughly 741 square kilometres. Kempegowda, born in 1510, was venerated as Nadaprabhu Kempe Gowda and left Kannada inscriptions across the region; the circle that carries his name grew around the Gavigangadeshwara Temple, the rock-cut shrine on Gavipuram hill that he is said to have built or renewed.

The Pete's trading quarters took their names from the trades practised in them, from grain at Tharagupete to flowers at Tigalarapete.
The old Pete covered about 2.24 square kilometres around the mud fort Kempegowda built as its nucleus.

landmarks.name: Kengeri Lake (Kengeri Sagara)
landmarks.subcategory: Peri-urban tank in the Vrishabhavathi basin
landmarks.description: A small peri-urban tank on Mysore Road at Kengeri in far western Bengaluru, developed by the state forest department in 1995 and lying in the headwater reach of the Vrishabhavathi river. The shallow, silted water body sits in largely open scrub a few hundred metres from the Kengeri Bus Terminal metro station and has long been awaiting a second rehabilitation attempt.
landmarks.history:
Kengeri Lake, also listed as Kengeri Lake (Doddakere), lies on Mysore Road in western Bengaluru and was developed by the state forest department in 1995. Wikipedia's inventory of Bengaluru lakes places the tank at 12.9163 N, 77.4874 E with an area of 38 acres, and the BBMP custodian list of Bengaluru lakes records it as Kasaba Kengeri Kere in the Kengeri ward. It sits in the headwater reach of the Vrishabhavathi river system, which runs south from this part of the city towards the Arkavathi.

The surrounding Kengeri locality takes its name from Kannada words for coconut and a place of trees, and carries a Chola inscription of 1050 AD at the Eshwara Temple; Kengeri Fort is associated with Tipu Sultan and was destroyed by the British. As of September 2018 the Deccan Herald reported that Kengeri Lake was still waiting for a second attempt at revival. The Purple Line metro stations Pattanagere, Kengeri Bus Terminal and Kengeri were inaugurated on 29 August 2021, with services starting the following day.

landmarks.name: Koramangala
landmarks.description: Koramangala is a south-east Bengaluru locality of tree-lined roads, bungalows and low-rise apartments that became a commercial centre and a prominent startup hub during the technology boom. It is laid out in eight blocks that straddle the Inner Ring Road, which separates Blocks 1-4 from Blocks 5-8. The 80 Feet Road corridor links the blocks and carries the neighbourhood's restaurants, cafes and offices.
landmarks.history: Koramangala was planned as a suburban area after independence; until the 1970s travellers commonly bypassed it, and housing expanded in the late 1970s. Its position between Bengaluru and Electronic City attracted migrants from across India during the city's technology boom in the late 1990s, when it transformed into a major commercial and business destination. The eight blocks cover roughly 1,800 acres, with the Inner Ring Road separating Blocks 1-4 from Blocks 5-8. The neighbourhood's rise coincided with Electronic City's growth as an IT hub, with companies such as Infosys based there.

landmarks.name: Magrath Road
landmarks.description: Magrath Road is a short commercial street in central Bengaluru, in the Sampangi Rama Nagar and Ashok Nagar block immediately behind Mayo Hall, and is part of the nineteenth-century Cantonment street grid. It is named after Colonel John Richard Magrath of the Royal Madras Artillery, and historically served as 'the stomping ground of the British military elite'; today it is a busy retail and services street known for the traffic jams at the Garuda Mall approach. OpenStreetMap records roughly 930 metres of named carriageway here, with the Mallya Hospital and the District Court complex close by.
landmarks.history: The street formed part of the ordered Cantonment grid laid out when the British military and its families settled in Bangalore after 1809, and it was named for Colonel John Richard Magrath of the Royal Madras Artillery, who later became an Assistant to the Director-General of Telegraphs; after retiring from Bangalore to Ireland he reputedly owned the only car then in Ireland, a 3.5 hp Benz Dogcart registered MI 1. Its western end is anchored by Mayo Hall, the two-storey memorial to Viceroy Richard Bourke, built in 1878-79 and inaugurated by the British Resident on 6 June 1883 at a cost of about 45,000 rupees raised largely through public donations. In more recent times the street has been the subject of a municipal facelift: The Times of India reported a 'new look' with wider footpaths and better drains across a 350-metre stretch.

Mayo Hall now houses the municipal offices of the Bruhat Bangalore Mahanagara Palike and the Kempegowda Museum, established in 2011 on the upper floor.
The Times of India reported a 2025 facelift of the street with wider footpaths and improved drains across a 350-metre stretch.

landmarks.name: Mahatma Gandhi Road (MG Road) Metro Station
landmarks.description: Mahatma Gandhi Road station - MG Road to everyone who uses it - is an elevated station on the east-west Purple Line of Namma Metro, standing on the boulevard at the western end of what was once the city's main shopping street. It opened with the first section of the network on 20 October 2011. Building the metro meant taking up the road entirely: the old MG Road boulevard was demolished and rebuilt, and the reconstruction was contracted to the Rajiv Gandhi Rural Housing Corporation and the Karnataka Land Army Corporation, with parts of it reopened in September 2012. The rebuilt boulevard spreads over about 850 square metres and is planned as a two-tier walkway whose ground floor carries a museum, an art gallery, an amphitheatre and a children's play area, with the first floor linking up to the station concourse.
landmarks.history: The old MG Road boulevard was demolished to make way for Namma Metro. Reconstruction was contracted to the Rajiv Gandhi Rural Housing Corporation and the Karnataka Land Army Corporation with a March 2012 deadline, but the ground was found to be unstable and had to be reinforced, so the work ran late. The new boulevard cost Rs 50 million, and portions of it were inaugurated on 5 September 2012. The station itself was constructed by Punj Lloyd.

landmarks.name: Malleswaram (Malleshwaram)
landmarks.description: One of Bengaluru's oldest neighbourhoods and its 'cultural heart', Malleswaram is a dense north-central residential locality laid out on a rectilinear grid of 1st and 8th Main Roads. It is anchored by the 17th-century Kadu Malleshwara Temple and by a busy street market that supplies the whole north of the city with oil, millets and provisions. The area also holds the Indian Institute of Science and, at its southern edge, the World Trade Center Bengaluru.
landmarks.history: The area was conquered by Shahaji Bhonsle, a general of the Bijapur Sultanate, during the first half of the 17th century, and Ekoji I, Shahaji's son, donated the village of Medaraninganahalli - near today's Indian Institute of Science - to the Kadu Malleshwara Temple. Inscriptions dated 1669 call the locality 'Mallapura', and a Kannada inscription found near Sampige Road is recorded in Epigraphia Carnatica. The name was absent from British records: the Survey of India in 1878 placed the site inside Ranganathapalya village. In 1889 Maharaja Chamaraja Wodeyar X appointed a committee headed by K. Seshadri Iyer to relieve congestion in central Bengaluru; that committee planned Malleshwaram and Basavanagudi, with Malleshwaram initially covering 291 acres. The committee ended in 1895, when the municipality incorporated the neighbourhood into Bengaluru, and growth was initially slow - during the 1896 plague epidemic health authorities set up camps and medical tents here, and many of the survivors settled permanently.
facts: Inscriptions dated 1669 call the locality 'Mallapura'; the Kadu Malleshwara Temple itself dates to 1669 CE and is built in the Dravidian style.
The Kadu Malleshwara Temple was built in 1669 by Venkoji, identified as the step-brother of the Maratha king Shivaji; the deity is Shiva worshipped as Mallikarjun.
The neighbourhood was planned by the 1889 K. Seshadri Iyer committee, which also laid out Basavanagudi, and initially covered 291 acres.
The committee was wound up in 1895 when the neighbourhood was incorporated into Bengaluru; during the 1896 plague epidemic the area hosted camps and medical tents for infected patients.

The locality covers 3.95 km2 with a population of 99,625 (2020), and contains the Indian Institute of Science, the Institute of Wood Science and Technology and the World Trade Center Bengaluru, described as the city's tallest commercial building.
The Kadalekai Parishe groundnut fair is held in Malleshwaram and Basavanagudi every November; in 2025 the Malleshwaram leg ran 8-10 November and more than 200 groundnut vendors took part.

landmarks.name: Russell Market
landmarks.description: Russell Market is a shopping market in the Bangalore Cantonment area of central Bengaluru, named after the municipal commissioner of the period. Built by the British and inaugurated in 1933, it is the city's best-known formal market building, with a predecessor market documented in photographs of the 1880s. Its location puts it between the Church Street and Commercial Street retail district and the government quarter around Cubbon Park.
landmarks.history: The market was built in 1927 by the British and inaugurated in 1933 by Ismail Sait, and named for the then municipal commissioner T. B. Russell. An archival photograph shows the predecessor market in the 1880s, with the spire of St. John's Church visible behind it. The market's covered blocks survived into the modern era but burned on 26 February 2012, when a fire gutted 123 shops and caused losses of 89.2 lakh rupees; the initial investigation attributed the blaze to a short circuit.

landmarks.description: Trinity is an elevated station on the east-west Purple Line of Namma Metro, a short walk from the Holy Trinity Church whose name it borrows, and the reason it is also called the Trinity Circle stop. It opened to the public on 20 October 2011 and was constructed by Punj Lloyd. What makes it unusual is the basement: in early 2016 BMRCL built a 4,000 square foot underground hall under the station, originally intended as storage, then reconsidered and let out to cultural groups. It has eighteen lights and a floor painted to form a stage, and can be rented by the hour through the metro office at MG Road.
landmarks.history: Trinity opened on 20 October 2011, built by Punj Lloyd. On 9 July 2014 BMRCL issued a tender to co-brand the station with a large corporation, the winner earning signage and a kiosk and having its name announced when the stop is called on board the trains. In early 2016 BMRCL constructed a 4,000 square foot basement beneath the station; it was first planned for storage, then rented out for cultural use, with eighteen lights installed and the floor painted to form a stage.
facts: Trinity is an elevated station on the east-west Purple Line and opened on 20 October 2011; it was built by Punj Lloyd.
A 4,000 square foot basement was built under the station in early 2016, originally for storage and then rented out to cultural groups.
The basement has eighteen lights and a floor painted to form a stage, and is rented at Rs 400 an hour through the metro office at MG Road.
In 2014 BMRCL tendered the station's co-branding to a large corporation, with signage, a kiosk and the name called on board the trains.

landmarks.name: Whitefield
landmarks.description: Whitefield is an east Bengaluru suburb that began as an Anglo-Indian agricultural settlement in 1882 and is today one of the city's principal IT corridors. The Export Promotion Industrial Park and International Tech Park (ITPL) form the business core, ringed by large residential apartment clusters that grew rapidly after 2002. It is also served by the Purple Line metro extension to Whitefield (Kadugodi) and by an electrified double-track railway line to Chennai.
landmarks.history: The locality began in 1882 as an agricultural settlement for Eurasians and Anglo-Indians, when Mysore's Maharaja Chamarajendra Wadiyar X granted 3,900 acres (16 km2) to the Eurasian and Anglo-Indian Association; it was named for David Emmanuel Starkenburgh White, president of the association and a promoter of the settlement. In the first decade of the 1900s Whitefield had about 45 houses, including 18 on the village site, and around 2,000 acres (8.1 km2) of cultivable land, with 130 residents recorded in 1907. A railway station was built about 3 km south of the settlement on the Bangalore-Madras line, drawing workers from the Kolar Gold Fields roughly 50 km to the east, with regular trains to Bangalore about 20 km west. Whitefield stayed a small village until the late 1990s, when Bengaluru's technology boom transformed it into a major suburb, with residential construction surging from the latter half of the 1990s and particularly from 2002.
facts: The settlement was founded in 1882 when Maharaja Chamarajendra Wadiyar X granted 3,900 acres (16 km2) to the Eurasian and Anglo-Indian Association.
It was named for David Emmanuel Starkenburgh White, president of the association and a promoter of the settlement.
In the first decade of the 1900s there were about 45 houses (18 on the village site), roughly 2,000 acres (8.1 km2) of cultivable land, and 130 residents in 1907.
A railway station was built roughly 3 km south of the settlement on the Bangalore-Madras line, attracting workers from the Kolar Gold Fields about 50 km east.

The Export Promotion Industrial Park and International Tech Park (ITPL) became major technology centres, with offices including Mercedes-Benz's R&D centre, Caterpillar at RMZ NXT and Societe Generale.
The Purple Line extension from Krishnarajapura to Whitefield (Kadugodi) runs 13.71 km with 13 intermediate stations; it was inaugurated on 25 March 2023 and opened to passengers on 26 March 2023.

landmarks.name: The Leela Palace, Bengaluru
landmarks.description: The Leela Palace is a 357-room luxury hotel on HAL Old Airport Road in the Kodihalli area of Bengaluru, part of The Leela Palaces, Hotels and Resorts chain. It draws on Indo-Saracenic architecture inspired by the Mysore Palace: it is built in pink sandstone and has copper domes, marble columns and large windows, and sits in about nine acres of landscaped gardens whose sculptures include the Yali, the mythical creature common in South Indian temple architecture. It opened in 2001 and in 2019 became part of the portfolio acquired by Brookfield Asset Management from Hotel Leelaventure Limited.
landmarks.history: The hotel was developed by Hotel Leelaventure Limited and opened on Old Airport Road in 2001, the group's third hotel after The Leela Mumbai and The Leela Goa. It began with a soft launch on 16 August 2001 with 71 rooms, then opened in phases to its full capacity. In 2019 The Leela Palace Bengaluru was among the hotels acquired by Brookfield Asset Management from Hotel Leelaventure Limited, and ownership was consolidated under Schloss Bangalore Limited. It is a member of the Global Hotel Alliance and Preferred Hotels & Resorts.
facts: The Leela Palace has 357 rooms and opened in 2001 on Old Airport Road, in the Kodihalli area.
It was developed by Hotel Leelaventure Limited and soft-launched on 16 August 2001 with 71 rooms before opening in phases.
In 2019 it joined the portfolio acquired by Brookfield Asset Management, with ownership consolidated under Schloss Bangalore Limited.
The architecture is Indo-Saracenic, inspired by the Mysore Palace, in pink sandstone with copper domes, marble columns and large windows.
The hotel sits within about nine acres of landscaped gardens decorated with Yali sculptures.
It is a member of the Global Hotel Alliance and Preferred Hotels & Resorts.
